div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

The International Railway Congress at the end l of the month is to be a great representative gather- ing. It may he said that the railway systems of the world will be represented. The delegates will come from 50 countries, and that means the four I quarters ot the globe. Nearly eery railway system, in Europe will send at least one delegate, and the I pettiest Engli.h company is sure to have a repre- sentative present Altogether, the number of rail- I way undertakings which will be in evidence is 'lose upon 300. Papers will he read and discussions carried on, and there will be excursions to various parts of the country to examine the works of tha leading lines. It. is interesting to notice from the programme that, the nglish railway managers are taking in a more kindly way to light railways than, according to Mr Chaplin, the English landlords are I likely to do.

The first of the dog show exhibits, at which are only to be the property of laities,was an extraordin- ary success. It was held at the Ratielagh Club. Barns Elms, and was attended by almost. the whole of London Society, including the Prince and Princess of W ales. The Castelaun and Putney roads leading to the club were crowded with carriages the whole afternoon, and the subrcription list is so promising that another show is to be held next year, not necessarily in London. It was such a success that it would be right to get up such shows in the country. The Princess of Wales is an immense lover of dogs. and she went round the hundreds of animals on• Saturday, giving biscuits to one and a friendly pat on the head to others.

It is said that Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone desire to see St. Petersburg after their visit to Kiel, as neither of them has ever visited the Russian capital. As the Czar has the greatest admiration for Mr. Gladstone, there is only one obstac:e in the way— time. The story told is that Mr. Gladstone particularly desires the trip, and that he will be gratified.

No reporter seems et to have investigated the fate of the soap which, unless rumour lied, was provided in large quantities for the use of the Shahzada at Dorchester House. There is an un- corroborated story, repeated by the " Realm," that when the Shah was here a member of his staff ale the whole of a cake of soap which had been thoughtlessly left in his bedroom. According to the "Realm," the son of the Ameer is terribly shocked at the low-necked dresses worn by Eng- lish ladies. At a recent party (it is said by t hose who know the Oriental countenance) he blushed deeply many times. The Court Ball must have dis- tressed him still more. Afghanistan is not like India, in some parts of which ladies are in full Court dress if they have on a bead necklace. If a gentleman there has on a pair of white gloves only he is considered to be completely attired. Occasion- ally he puts a few feathers in his hair; but that is when he is given to over-dressing.

Paving regard to the nature of recent events, it is very significant to hear that a French agent who was in St. Petersburg ha ,3 just been entrusted by the Russian Government with orders tor military and naval supplies ot a very extensive character. The orders were sealed, and the agent was com- manded to transmit them direct to two firms in France, one of which is known for its powders, the other being a leading ship building yard. The matter, I learn, involves business to the extent of something like 60,000,00 G francs—say .£2,400,000 sterling.

• The guess that the occult cause of Lord Bose- bevy's present cruise about the Channel is to study for him.elf the possibility of buying uffour troubles with France in Canada and Africa by a transference to that Power of alloy some of the Channel Islands is an ingenious speculation. The surrender of Heligoland to Germany by the late Tory Govern- ment, in exchange for some African Territory, is a very suggestive case in point, and gives the" deal" an air of possibility. Then there is the fact that England and France are drifting daily into rela- tions which may at any moment end in a rupture between the two countries. The Channel Islands I are of no value to us, and would be, of little to ' France, except that they ought to belong to her by geographical and political gravitation. Unquestion- ably. French sentiment vt culd be immensely gratified at their possession. In the event cf war we could not bold the islands ; they would be one of the first prizes that would fall into the hands of the enemy. They would not be worth the life of a single bluejacket, except as a mere matter of ra-,ional honour. They are only a few miles from the French coast. An agreement might be effected it we abandoned Egypt, but until. the Fgyptian question is out of the way, even the Channel Islands would be regarded by French politicians as very poor compensation to France for what she would be expected to give up.

Judging by the tone in Unionist quarters there does not appear to be much likelihood of anything being done from the_upposition benches to bring about a crisis at present. The Unionist members who have been urging their leaders to take the ini- tiative in a discussion on the state of procedure hare met with very little encoutagement. It is perfectly evident that Mr. Balfour and most of his colleagues are averse from doing anything to force matters at the present time. Probably the only members on the Conservative benches who would 1 teeny like to begin an active attack on the Government just now are the Irish landlord party, who would be glad of anything likely to wreck the I Land Bill. But it is certainly not Mr. Balfour's I vame to let this Bill be wrecked if he can help it.

One of Mr. Gladstona's intimate associates assures me that the right hon. gentleman is still plagued with almoi.t as great a volume of correspondence as when he was in office. Since his retirement tram public life there has, indeed, been some increase in the number of letters sent to hi by persons who desired the autograph of the aged •statesman, or write risking his opinion on public questions. or send hooks which they hoped he may now have leisure to read. In the 'hope of abating this nuis- ance Mr. Gladstone has issued one more appeal to the public not to write to him, especially during his absence from England. •

?Ir. Balfour, writes a corn spondent, is not a very graceful cyclist. His length and his " scholarly stoop " militate against pretty riding, and those who have seen him on the bicycle say that he looks much better on the golf links.

_ In Australia, a few months back, numbers of correspondents set themselves I he task of discover- ing the "champion mean man" and reporting on his peculiarities. Some of them would have gained a place in the competition had they known a musi- cal artist whose top notes are at this moment much discussed in London. The notes of his ex- chequer run higher even than the notes of his voice, fur his banking balance is good for almost a quarter of a million. Not many weeks ago he was one of a party of artists entertained by the Mil- lionaires' Club in America, and during the feast it was noticed by some that this wealthy songster's hands mode ftequent mysterious dives under the , table.

--- The cause was apparent a little later when he rose from the table and hurried to his cab with a serviette full of delicacies from his host's board, and which be explained'were " for his dear." On another occasion, at a smart ode, cutlets 4 la Mil- anese were the 'lee de resistenee, and at the close of the repast the singer asked for a piece of paper,and in this he wrapped the surplus cutlets, to the dis- may of his colleagues, to whom be remarked," For my little dog ; for my little dog." A few hours later one of his colleagues called at the rooms of the wealthy singer, and found him making his evening meal on the cutlets taken for the dog!

At the invitation of Mr. Arnold Morley several members of Parliament—mostly members of the Telephone Committee—were present on Wednes- day at the inauguration of the trunk telephone lines between London and Scotland and Ireland. Amongst those in attendance were Sir Charles Cameron, Mr. Snape, and Mr. 0. Lawson. Messages of congraulation were exchanged by the Postmas- ter General and the Lord Mayor of London with the Lord Provost of Glasgow and Fdinburgh, and with the Lord Mayors of Dublin and Belfast. The voices were in every case distinctly heard, and the experiments were considered to be highly suc- cessful.

I At M'Alpine, in Florida, on Monday, a negro was lynched for an attempted aggravated assault on a white woman, and two other negroes who aided him in an at- tempt to escape from justice were shot. All three bodies were afterwards carried to a railway and laid on the metals,where they were terribly mangled by passing trains.

Of one thousand persons only one reaches the age o one hundred years, and not more than biX that of s five years. The highest temperature in the world is recorded in the great desert of Africa, where the thermometer often marks one hundred and fifty degrees Fahrenheit. It may be interesting to know that in moving from one place to another the pPople of this country spend about one hundred and fifty thousand pounds a thy. A statement was made in a London police court that the meatal disease of a domestic had communicated itself to her mistress, the wife of a medical man. According to an Anglo-American paper, Mrs, Commo- dore Garrison is now the only remaining very rich American widow residino, in London. To wash silk ties, boil half a pound of bran in a quart of water for an hour, and then strain. Wash the ties in this water, keeping them quite i.traight ; rinse in salted water, and iron while slightly damp. There is a considerable difference between the size of the hands and feet, and, curimsly enough, on opposite sides. Thus, whilst the right hand is generally the larger, it is the left foot which is the bigger and stronger of the two. This is probably due to the fact that we stand habitually on the left foot. If a can of milk is placed near an open vessel contain- ing turpentine the smell of turpentine will be soon com- municated to the mi'k. The same result occurs as re- gards tobacco, paraffinosafce'ida, camphor, and many other strong-smelling subs, ances. Milk shrell I alio ha kept at a distance from every volatile substance, and that which has stood in sick chambers should never be drunk. Lace is a fabric that can be made to represent large amounts of na nay, rhe Astors have been credited with owning lace worth six hundred thousand pounds, and the Vanderbilts values their laces at eight hundr, d thousand pornds. The Pope is said to be con- tent with only fifteen thousand pounds represented in lace, and the Princess of Wales can boast of fifty thou- sand pounds' worth of the daiaty fabric. The veil which Princess fliS'ene will wear on her wPd- ding-dav was made at Bayeux and is a beautiful speci- men of French lace. It is three yards and a half long. and has a lovely border of exquisitely worked fliwers. In the middle are the fam'ly arms of the bride and thoQe of the bridegroom, together with three French lilies forming a background. It shoulel be universally known that sand or fi ,ur scattered over burning oil will extinguish it. Every household in which lamps are used should have a small box filled with sand in some convenient corner, ready for all emergencies. It has the great advantage ov, r flour in being heavy,and not easily affected by draughts or currents of air.

Dangerous Domestic Practice. It is a common custom for cooks to place jellies on a window ledge or some such place to cool. This is a most dangerous practice. When a bacteriologist wants to secure minute organisms for Investigation, he exo as gelatine to the air or in places where he has confined malignant germs. The gelatine speedily attracts and holds them. The flivoured gelatine does the same. Cool the jelly if you must, but cover it with a piece of close muslin. It is to be feared that kitchen processes are sources of illness more often than is imagined. In many houses the little kitchen and the pantvy where various eatables are kept, is directly against a drain. Yet here stand daily unc...vered milk, butter, often cus- tards and puddings, and various other absorbents. The average cook is absolutely ignorant of sanitary cause and effect, and the eternal vigilance of the house mother is the family's chief safeguard.

The season of flies is at hand. Both the common and hlo sg-fly are great pegts. Much damage may be pre- vented by destroying them at the proper season. t%,• soon as swarms appear in the windows sweep them with a soft brush into a bajn of boiling water. Ply-paper sold by chemists is very useful. It is not safe to use any poisonous liquid to destroy flies. They may din their feet into it and carry it where it will do harm. The fol- lowing composition is effic.icious, and can be used with- out fear of injury. Mix well one teaspoonful of black pepper, two teaspoonfuls of moist sugar, and two table- spoonfuls of cream. Place a little of it in a sAucer where the flies abound. No flies will go near any place where creosote is kept.

Airing Bed and Body Linen. The airing of bed and body linen is a very important item in the household management. Many are the lives that have been ruined and even sacrificed thrnugh wa,t of care in this respect,. It is a matter which should never be left entirely in the rare of seivants. Laun- dresses often send clothes home in a very damp condi- tion, and some are apt to think that if they are all placed over a clothes horse tether, and allowed to re- main an hour or so in a warm room, that is sufficient. This, however, is not at all the case. Flannel garments and thick calico with pleats or folds in them r, (Ore to be pliced near a good fire for some time. Sheets require to he well spread out and well turned before the lire. One can easily f,el if any dimpness remains b passinz the hand inside and all over the aired sheets. When refolded and ready to be put avrar, he sure they are put in a perfectly dry receptacle until they are require.%

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

The short capes, on account of their extreme convenience, are likely, I feel sure, to remain in fashion for some time. Capes are still wide at the edge, but less so than they have been of late, and they fall smoothly over the shoulders. For the spring they are made of cloth, velvet, and silk, but in a very short time there will be some lovely little capes for summer wear, all fluffy with ruches of lace or flounces of gauze, and finished off with a still shorter overeape of embroidered silk or velvet, cut all round the edge in long sharp points, or else in rounded scallops. Single capes in ' lace, or embroidered material and lace, are charm- ingly trimmed with bows of ribbon on the collar and shoulders. Opera cloaks and delightful little capes can be made of a, few yards of silk brocade and a little lace, or of velvet, with an overcape of cloth or silk in a lighter colour, cut in pointed or square tabs, and embroidered with black, steel, or :gold sequins. An upright collar, standing out tram the neck, is usually cut in one with the over- :cape, and in some models long ends of chiffon or ,silk muslin fall in front from the neck. There are some very pretty jackets to be seen. One I liked very much had a large sailor collar i made in cloth of a pretty shade. The jacket, I which was. close-fitting, was made of brown Venetian cloth, and had the fashionable bishop sleeves. The pockets and the cuffs to the sleeves were also in a pretty cloth. There were three large pearl buttoes. A masculine collar and tie should be worn, of course, with this jacket, and a iailor hat. The parasol may be of red shot silk.

_ all colours and mat,. __.,. A pretty one is made of lilac zephyr, with finely- pleated frills of white cambric edging the wide collar,, and forming a ruffle down the front. I should not advise anyone whose laundress is not "a real treasure" to have the elaborately ruffled front, which is most difficult to iron properly. A nice design, easily made at home, is of a cross-over shape, with a yoke. The chief difficulty is to see fat the fitting lining is well-made, and that the full fronts are 'draped on the figure. It is for bodices of this kind that the dress-stands, made to measurements of one's own figure, are so very con- venient, they save so much of the wearisome trying on process. Two and a half yards of crepon or nun's veiling, and threequarters of a yard of surah for the pleated vest would be sufficient for this. blouse. Tea-gowns are, some of them, very elaborate. A fashionable one I saw lately was of a pretty pale blue crepon. The sleeves were long hanging ones, and terminated in points with large satin bows and ends. There was a large jabot in front.

In the way of millinery, the first thing that strikes me is the extraordinary number and diver- sity of the fancy straws which are being shown for the spring. The plaits are most elaborate, both straw and rush bring used, and the colours are many and varied, either used separately or together, in many mixtures. The edges of all are orna- mented, generally with upstanding loops; and there is a great widening of all the new headgear over the forehead: and, in fact, a general impres- sion of an increase of size, which is however, owing in part to the immense amount of trimming, garlands, and wreaths of flowers in all hues. Rosettes of ribbon, jet, lace, and feathers are all used on one bottnet, and flowers completely cover the surface of many others of those which are seen. There is no doubt of our having plenty of colour this year in all our apparel, and yet there is a very distinct tendency in favour of black in every department of dress, and certainly amongst French models. But it is generally united with one colour' or even two. Green straw is coming into vogue for hats. It is usually made coarse. A

hat in this material is striped with rays of narrow black velvet ribbon, and flanked with choux bows in giten openwork straw ribbon. There is a con- spicuous aigrette of black paradise birds, with Ispreys, and feathers. - Yours lovingly, theiNTE.

div.head: POLITICAL BORES.
div.p: POLITICAL BORES.

WHAT LORD ROSEBERY HAS TO PUT UP WITH. During the recent inrlispo,itinn of Lord Rosebery, no less than one hundred cures for insomnia were sent to 1394k1ey-sqoare, all warranted to lull the sleepless Pre- mier to rest. • Th..ffi ,i4ls at Downinz-st. d their best to lighten tha labours of their chief. When the correspondence which is not " PriVate and Con fid intial " has been read, a piece of coloured paper is affixed to each document to denote its degr p of urgency. If red, the matter will wait ; if yellow as soon as poSsihle ; it gremiircent and of vital importance. Stfll Private and Confidential has to be respected ; and to awe try !Moister it must be terribly trying to open twenty letters in succession either from angry or fawning supplicants, or from weak- kneed followers who warn him that their conscience will not permit them, &!., &c. During the last forty years it is stated that over twenty thousand letters have been received at Downing- t. showing how the Nati Dual Debt might be paid off. Quite a numbv of people for the last two years have been warning Lord Rosebery that a secret coalition is being formed by the great Continental Powers • to destroy the Prestige of England. The warnings vary in style. One after bluntly declaring that Ministers will be false to their duty if they neglect making themselves acquainted with these eandes•ine designs' will nobly place his ser- vices at his country's disposal, winding up with a sug- gestion that a secret mission under his control would be the hest plan, the Crown, of co rse, defraying all expenses. some adopt a much more mysterious tone. I am assured that just before he embarked on his recent Channfl cruise Lord Rosebery received a letter from a trembling patrint,in which be was solemnly assured that the writer was in possession of information of Such vital importance to the realm that he dared not commt it to paper. "Would his brdsl.ip, therefore, on grounds of pressing Imperial need, gran him on interview ?" Shortly before the recent China-Japan war,•the Foreign Office was literally bombarded with letters from all parts of England advising how we should comport oursrlvea during the affray. Strange to say, tke only writer who predicted the result of the struggle, mapped out the events which subsequently happened with such curious accuracy that it is not unlikely that some employment will be found for this gentleman's atilities.

CHAPTER XXXIV. FREDERICK THORNTON S WIFE.

" How foolish I alit to he so agitaLed at tne name —Frederick, ' thought Doris, re, overing her com- posure by a violent eilort. "Of course there is snore ihan one 'Frederick' in the world." Alt, how she loved the handsome young husband whom she was, even then, hiding from. All her Wea t h seemed dross to her, because she had missed Fiederick Thornton's love. By a great .4t,rt Doris collected her scattered thoughts, and listened to what the old nurse was saying : 'Are you ill, child? Why, you are as white as a ghost." " No, I am not ill," replied Doris ; " it was only a sudden pain at my heart. Pray go on; I am lis7ening to your story.' And the old nurse did go on with the strange revelation that was to change, the current of two lives. "As I was saying," she continued, "time whole family of the rich banker was very grateful for the excellent care I had taken of hands° ie Mr. Fred- erick, and I iz;ew to know them well—so well that when I was transferred front Baltimore to the New York hospital, I stopped a week at their beamti ul home. "And it was then that I heard the tragic story that has darkened poor Mr. Frederick's life ever since the hour of that fatal sickness." Doris was beginning to feel strangely interested in the narrative. Site could n t tell why. She was listening intently, her hands locked tightly together in her hip, her large blue eyes never leav- ing the old nurse's face. "I told you of the blank in poor Mr. Frederick's mind when he left the hospital," she continued, " a,ld of something which he feli had escaped from his memory, try hard as he wo hl to recall it. He could not even remember what had brought him to Baltimore, or why he was there." "Yes, you told that before,'' said Doris, impa- tient at the repetition. "Upon that hangs the tragedy which followed," answered the nurse, wiping a tear from her eye with her long white apron. "Poor Mr. Frederick went back to his home, and his mother and sisters and his old sweetheart, who was visiting there, gave the Alol of the family a royal welcome. It was almost like having him back. from the grave—he had been so near the borders of eternity. " This sweetheart was a pretty, dark-eyed girl, why thought a heap of Master Frederick, and the great rues she made over his return flattered his vanity, of course. He never knew before quite how much she cared for him. " When he asked her to marry him, and she consented, nothing could have pleased his family

more. "The day was set for the wedding, the bride's trousseau was ordered, the invitations for the grand wedding were t.4iven out, and the day set for the marriage was fast drawing near. "Then suddenly, and without warning, the strangest event happened that ever happened in any young man's lite. "One evening, while walking with his sweet- heart, he was suddenly confronted by a young and beautiful girl, who claimed him as her husband. A great gasp broke from Doris's white lips; but the old nurse, not heeding it, went on, slowly : "The young girl claimed him crying out that she had tracked him down at last—the young husband who had married her, and had deserted her almo•t at the altar." Again that horrible gasp broke from Doris's lips, and was unnoticed. Doris tried to speak, to cry out, but the words died away in her throat. The room, the green trees outside the window, and the face of the old nurse seemed whirling around her; and through it all, as if shrieked out, trumpet- tongued, upon the still air, she could hear every word that was uttered. "Then, in a flash—that which Mr. Frederick had tried so hard all in vain to recall when he recovered Irons his dangerous illness, came back to him. And it struck him dumb with horror. • "It was quite true. He had married the lovely young girl, bringing her to Baltimore on their wi ding trip; and stepping out to get a cigar, the terrible accident had occurred which 1 .id him up for long weeks in the hospital. And, oh, the pity of it ! Think of it l—picture it 1 When he had recovere ~ it was with a strange blank in his mind. He had forgotten the existence of the fair young bride he had brought to Baltimore forgot his marriage and all connected wi ii it. And it was all the more pitiful, because it had been a secret one. Even his relatives knew nothing of it. , "Before he could find voice, in his horor, grief and amazement, to explain this to the young bride who believed herself so cruelly deserted, arid had tracked him down, finding him about. to . wed another, she had lied, and—" The rest of the entence never was finished. With the wildest cry ever heard, Doris pracg from the couch, and sank down in a dead fadtt at the old nurse's feet. In an instant she had raised the slim, girlish figure in her strong arms, and laid her on the couch again. "Dear me ! who would have thought the story would have affected her so!" she muttered, brush- ing ba.,-k the lovely, clinging golden curls from the marble white face. "I only meant to draw her thoughts away from her own troubles. I aim afraid this will throw the poor child back ter- ribly." She lost no time in administering restoratives, and soon the lovely blue eyes opened, and they rested on the old nurse's face; there was a gleam so strangely bright in them that Mrs. Linwood, the old nurse, was quite frightened. With a great sob Doris struggled up to a sit- ting posture and caaght eagerly at the old nurse's hands. "Was it a dream ?" she cried, incoherently. "Tell me—was it a dream?" " Was what a dream, my dear?" asked the old nurse, in puzzled wonder, looking in affright at the girl's flushed face. "That it was fate that separated Frederick and me !" gasped Doris. "That he did not mean to de..ert me so heartlessly I Oh, there has been a most horrible mistake—a mistake that has wrecked two lives I" she cried out, incoher,ntly. " Listen, nurse," she cried, vehemently. "I am that most unhappy bride who wedded Frederick Thornton secretly and came with him to Balti- more, and who had every reason to believe that he had wilfully delerted me.'' " You!" cried the old nurse in the greatest amazement. "Yes, I," repeated Doris, sobbing as though her heart would break. "It must have been the hand of fate that led me to you, nurse, and prompted you to reveal to me Frederick Thornton's story. And oh! the joy of knowing he never meant to be false to me ! Oh, nurse, nurse, those words have made me well Mrs. Linwood almost believed it as she looked at the girl's beautiful flushed face, and her eyes bright as stars. Long a ral earnestly the old nurse and Doris talked the mat er over; and Doris told her all of her piti- ful story from beginning to end. "Now that you know all, nurse," sire sobbed faintly, "what would you advise me to do?' Oh, how eagerly, wistfully the lovely blue eyes scanned the wrinkled face of the old nurse who had saved Frederick's life. Mrs. Linwood took the alto, white, trembling hands in her own, and smiled down into the eager, lovely young face. "There is bet One thing to say, my dear," she answered, slowly, "and that is—to go back to your husband.': D^ri'l drew back with a sudden blush. •• Nay, nay; do hot lot false modesty stand ite6ween you now,' she counselled. " You are his lawfuld, wed.l4-d. wife; and a wife's place is by tier husband's side." "Oh, nurse, if you would but send for Frederick to come to me, telling him all," sobbed Doris, hid- ing her lovely face on the pillow. "I know a better way," declared Mrs. Linwood. "As soon as you are strong enough to stand the little journey I will take you to him. He is now at Thornton Villa," she answered.
CHAPTER XXX V. DORIS GOES TO FREDERICK'S ROME.

IT has often been said that "Love works won- ders." This was especially true in Doris's case. From that moment her rapid convalescence was most wonderful. In a week's time she was able to undertake the short journey to Thornton Villa. "How strange it seems—going back to my—my —husband, a ter being so strangely parted from him three long years ago ;" 8 id Doris, clinging to her e0ne..e,0., ann, nif Isogh.ng and haq :Lbill:2; the
streets, then struck into the shady read that rid

, out into the suburbs. Oh, how joyously the birds warbled, looking at the lovely face in the carriage that whirled by, with their bright little eyes, as much as to say : " We know where you are going ; we hope you will have a royal welcome.' Even the flowers seemed to nod gaily to Doris from the roadside as she passed them. "Every mile brings me nearer to my love," mur- mured Doris, as she counted the mile stones. And yet, when the great turrets and towers of Thornton Villa loomed up in the distance before her, she grasped litT companion's arm with nervous
. _ dread. "1 am coming to Frederick's home uninvited," she breathed, softly. "I wonder if his mother and sisters will be glad or sorry when they see

me !" Then she remembered under what widely dif- ferent auspices she had crossed that threshold before. She blushed to remember it—in disguise, and as his mother's paid companion. Now her fortunes were strangely reversed. She was heiress to a million now; a courted, petted society belle—a different personage, indeed, from the little nobody, the poor little dependent whom Mrs. Thornton wo,ild have considered no match for her

handsome, eie,ont son. "Of course they will be glad to see you, my dear," declared the old nurse, warmly. "They know but too well how Mr. Frederick has mourned and grieved after you." Trembling with excitement, she still clung to the old nurse's arm as the carriage swept up the long curved drive to the porch. Mrs. Thornton and her three daughters, Isabel, Gwendoliu and Trixy, were seated in the drawing. room engaged in quite a spirited discussion at that particular moment. And it hail all been brought about by a letter Gwendolin he!' in her hand. It was from Vivian Carsdale, and said in the postscript that she in- tended paying them a flying visit some time during the following week—"and had something wonder- ful to tell them—that is, if you have not learned all about it from Frederick i-re this," she added. And it was as to what this wonderful news could be they were just then discussing. "1 hope my brother has not married that artful Vivian at last," e; ied Trixy, an! I am almost sure it is that; for did not Frederick write us himself nearly six weeks ago, these incidental words—' he had something wonderful to tell us, when he came home'?" "I used to think BO much of Vivian, three years ago," sighed Mrs. Thornton. "It was the one desire of my life to see her Frederick's wife—and now I am only too thankful that they drifted asunder." "Perhaps the artful young widow has accom- plished that which the young girl failed to do— caught Frederick in her toils after all," said Isabel. "What if it shoul I be about Gerald Marston, the old lover whom Vivian threw over for Frederick three years ago, would you care, Gwendolin 7" asked Trixy, looking roguishly at her sister. She could say nothing about him that could affect me," said Gwendolin Thornton, proudly. " She might say that she had met him again, and at sig,,t of her dark eyes the old flame of love has been re lighted in his breast, and he has laid his heart and fortune at her feet a second time.' "I should not believe it," returned Gwendolin, quietly. "All love for Vivian died out of Gerald's lie.f..rt long ago. He told me so only the last time he called. Oh, mamma," she cried, turning her blushing face toward her mother "shall I tell Isabel and Trixy what else he said ? ' she stam- mered, hiding her rosy face in her handkerchief. "I will tell them for you, my dear. They may as well know first as last smilea Mrs. Thornton. "Gerald asked your sister Gwendolin to become his wife, nay dears." There was a perfect shower of ohs and abs I from two pairs of lips, and in a trice, Isabel and Trixy were by their sister's side, covering her blushing face with kisses, declaring the era had stolen . mat eh on them. They had not even BUS- peeted such a tender state of affairs. "Then it ready must be our poor brother Fred- erick whom Vivian has caught in her toils," declared Trixy, despairingly. " He does not write much like a happy lover," said Isabel, languidly. "There is certainly a tone of despondency running through his letters." " Ah, mamma, you have almost forgotten to-day is Thursday," said Trixy. "You know Frederick is corning here to-day." "How could I f rget that, my dear ?" smiled Mrs. Thorntom "1 counting the hours until he arrives. He will not be here until seven. Ii is only three now, my dear," consultmg her jewelled watch. " I hear carriage wheels now, mamma,' declared Trixy, springing to the hay-window, from whence she had a very good view of the spiral drive that led to the front porch. " Yes, 1 sea a carriage. The coachman is opening du- door. It is not Frederick, main nia. Two ladie are alighting.'' tin g. " Callers," commented Mrs. ;Itornton, settling herself down in her chair and awaiting the inevit- able. " Why, bras me, if it'ien't old Nurse Linwood :" cried Trixy, from her post of idiservai.ion. " And there is beautiful young lady with her, mamma ; a young and very lovely lady, elegantly dressed.' Mrs. Thornton raised her eyebrows in surprise, but made no ckinnuent. _• _
. - A monwnt later there was the sound of voices in

the corridor without. Nurse Linwood and the but!er, who had never been on good terms, were having a little altercation outside. "Nd, ma'am, no; I cannot allow you and this lady to pass on to the drawing-:oom without being announced. My lady would be very angry, indeed "[lot I will pass on without being announced ?" declared Nurse- Linwood, emphatically. "Mrs. Thornton will never consider it presumption on my part, be sure of that." "Orders are orders, Mrs. Linwood," answered the man, sturdily. "All the ladies of the family are in the drawing-room, and perhaps' they might not like to be intruded upon by your forcing your way into,their presence. I ask you again to wait here until' I see whetner they will see you and this young womantor not." "Fiddlesticks t" snapped Nurse Linwood. "Stand out of the way, I say." "Do let the man announce us, nurse," whispered Doris "I would far rather do it than raise a scene;" but old Nurse Linwood was not to be shaken from her resolve. "See what is the matter, Trixy, my love," said Mrs. TM-rton, knitting her brows into a dark frown, "I cannot understand what those loud voices can mean. If Nurse Linwood is out there,. bid her to come in, by all means. Ah, Trixy, I can never repay the debt of gratitude I owe her. Her great care of him saved my darling boy's life."

Trixy flew to the door and flung it open. "Oh, it is you, is it, Nurse Linwood!" she called. "Come into the drawing-room." "Well, who has come out best now in the argu- ment ? ' said the old nurse to the butler, as she drew Doris triumphantly past him. But he was not to he outdone in this manner. "Mrs. Linwood—and—a lady I"' he announced, boldly, with a flourish of his hand. A moment later the old nurse and her charge had gained the threshold of the drawing-room. Instinctively M rs. Thornton and the young ladies had risen to their feet at the entrance of the graceful, veiled stranger Mrs. Linwood held by the hand. The next instant Doris had thrown up her veil. After three long years Frederick's mother and Doris stood face to face—at last ! For one instant a death-like silence reigned. Then Mrs. Thornton took a step forward, scanning breathlessly the lovely young face before her. "Who are you ? " she cried. "Your face is strangely familiar—and—yet—it is not I." The answer nearly took her breadth away. Doris came and knelt before her, bowing her lovely golden head as she replied: "I am your son's wife! / aim Doris 1" ( To be continued.)

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Councillr .1 'ales Fairclough), presided, and there were also present Alder- men Greenall, Francomh, Blackharst, Hutchinson, Sut- ton ; Councillors R. f. Fairclough, Roberts, ShAW. Green, Cannel!, Hill, Smethurst, Skelton, Siiiloock, Evans, Lee, Bennett, Shaw, Garner, Baird, Wilkinfon, Plumnton, Beaman, Monks, Heaton, rierp,int, Flew. herd, Longton, Davies, Wood ; Messrs. L Lyon Whittle (town clerk), S. Wilson (assistant town clerk), L.mg- clin (borough surveyor), Fairhurst (borough treat.urcr), and Ross (water engineer).

div.head: TUB LATE HR. JOSEPH TAILOR.
div.p: TUB LATE HR. JOSEPH TAILOR.
The MAYOR read a letter from Mrs. Taylor acknnw- ledging with thanks the vote of condolence on the death of her husband.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

1 The minutes of the following committees, as printed 'in the " Examiner " last week, was adopted with little or no discussion, viz. : Watch, Finance and Estates, Street Improvement, Health, Sanitary Works, Paving and Sewerage, School At'endance,Museum, Library and Arts, Markets and Cemetery 0.1 the minutes of the Health Committee, Councillor HEPHERD celled attenti to the bad state of the old portion ol the river between Wilderspool brewery and S. James' Church. For a fort- night past, he said, the river had been in a filthy state. —The MAYOR Come to Mersey Mills and we will give it you worse than it is there. (Laughter.)

div.head: TOWN HALL PARK AND BATHE COMMITTER.
div.p: TOWN HALL PARK AND BATHE COMMITTER.

—.— Councillor CANNELL in moving the minutes of this Committee said that he thought the increase in the re- ceipts of the bath was very satisfactory. fle also con- sidered that the £65 proposed for the erectiou of a new dressing room would be money well spent, as at present there was not sufficient accommodation.

Councillor GREEN did not agree with committees spending so many small sums. He did not think the present expenditure was called for. He would not move an amendment however. He only wished to draw atten- tioia to it. _ .

Councillor ROBERTS thought that it was desirable to have better accommodation fer the ladies' bith. Councillor HEATON as a member of the committee said they were willing to give all the accommodation they could in that small bath.

div.head: RNDUCTION IN THS_ PRICE OF .GAS,
div.p: RNDUCTION IN THS_ PRICE OF .GAS,

_ . Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH in moving the adoption of the minutes of this committee expre•aed satisfaction that the committee had been able to reduce gas 23. per thousand feet. He thought they had done exceedingly well last winter. The previous winter,the strike was on,and they did not raise the price of gas at that time although there was a small deficiency. When the question came up in committee this year to drop the price of gas, it was discussed as to whether to drop the priQe 23. or 33. per thousand, but it was considered that it would be far better to go slowly but surely,and therefore it was even- tually decided that it should be 23. per 1,000. The reserve fund at present was £5,000. Councillor BEPHERD seconded the adoption of the minutes. _

Councillor SMETHURST said that he was sure that everyone in Warrington was extremely obliged to the Gas Committee for reducing the price of gas, but they were not thankful that the gas bills rose ed perl,ooo. He knew of one workman whose gas bill had never been previously more that 255. and yet this time it was Ll. 18a. He could also speak of his own in similar terms. He knew of people who applied at the gas works for automatic meters but were refused. He thooght every- body had a perfect right to have those meters supplied to him if he desired it.

Ccuncillor BEAMAN thought the Gas Committee ought to he congratulated upon reducing the price of gas, and alsroupon gas being 5 per sent. better in the illuminating power. Councillor ROBERTS as a member of the Council to press the matter upon the consideration of the Gas Committee at the last meeting, was entirely glad that they had been able to make a small reduction. He hoped it was only an argury of what they might expect to continue from year to year. He was glad to join in the congratulations to the Gas Committee. Alderman SUTTON thought that the Council should be satisfied with the report gives them, considering that it meant a reduction eq la! to 10d. in the £ since they pur- chased the gas works. Considoring th4t the works re- presented a capital of £220,000, he did not think it at all unreasonable that any profit should he taken over to the reserve fond. A reserve fund of £5,000 was very small for an undertaking such as the gas works. Councillor PLuurrox asked the chairman of the com- mittee to tell the Council where they drew the line re- specting the slot system. He knew of persons who wished to have those meters placed in their houses, but they had been refused. It would be information to know where the line was drawn.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOITGR, in reply to Councillors Smethurst and Plumpton, said that there had been sr. many applications for meters that they could not supply automatic meters fast enough. Some people were ton fanciful and wished to try new things, and it would not be fair to have old meters left on the han 5 of the com- mittee.
The minutes WPTS then passed unsnimusly. RIVERS' COMMITTTE.-RF.SIGNIATION OF COUNCILLOR ROBERT FROM THE CHAIRMANSHIP.

The minutes of this committee appeared in our last issue and contained an agreement with NI ,ssrs. Bishop and Co. with reference to the construction of a wharf near Warrington Bridge, which the committee ree.om- mended for adoption, and also the appointment of the chairman of the committee as the representative upon the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. Councillor ROBERTS moved and Councillor HEATON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor HEPHERD moved as an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the eaceptinn of the above resolution,and that the resolution be referred back to the committee for consideration. He Objected to the Cor- poration parting with this frontage. In his opinion. they ought to retain it for their own benefit, and not he parties to introducing a common carrying traffic which would come into competition with the Ship Canal. (Hear, hear.)„. .
Alderman GREIENALL seconded the amendment. Councillors Woos and DAVIRS, and Aldermen SUTTON and BLILCIIHMIST supported the amendment.

Councillor Moiiims said that the opposition to the reso- lution was unreasonable. He pointed nut that the Cor- poration would have very little to pay for wharfage, as plans were being prepared fora larger Corporation wharf elsewhere. The land it was proposed to let to Messrs. Bishop and Co. would be of no use to any of the corn- mittees,and he saw no harm in the Corporation obt 4inlng some little return for the expense they had been put to in purchasing the rights from the Duchy of Lancaster. Councillor ROBERTS also thought that the agreement was very favourable to the Corporation. He himself would certainly not aclept the wharf under such an agreement as had just been read over,and it only showed an extraordinary amount of pluck and enterprise on the part of Messrs. Bishop and Co. in taking the wharf under such conditions. But the rnost important question was that they might be stifling at the very birth an enternr,se which was likely to be of considerable benefit to all the shcpkeepers and trader in the town. He trusted that the Council would not reject the proposal, for the terms and conditions were bound to be beneficial to the town generally. As to the idea that competition would he bad for the town,he held that the more competition they could produce between the parties, the better it would be for the town. If they thought the same, then there would not be one member round that table who would not vote for the passing of the minutes. The amendment was then voted upon and was carried by 18 votes to 7. Councillor HEPHERD then moved that the minute re- ferring to the appointment of the chairman to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Navigation Com- mission be also referred back to the committee. He thought that the services of Councillor Fairclough should be retained in that position. ' Alderman FRANCOMB seconded. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH explained that his reason for retiring from the position of chairman of the Rivers' Committee, some time ago was the fact that at that !time his firm was in dispute with the Manchester Ship Canal on the cpiestion of the abstraction of the water from the river used for the mills. Be bad felt that be could not conscientiously hold the office, and therefore retired, and Councillor Roberts took the seat he had vacated. But it was no reason why he should lose both his seat on the Rivers' Committee and the Commission, and he hoped that when the first vacancy occurred on the Rivers• Committee that he should be elected to it- Ho objected to being kicked out. If he must go, he would go properly, but would not submit to being quietly kicked out. Councillor ROBERTS said there was no kicking out about the matter at all. In the first place the Commis- sioner was appointed for three years. When that period expired the Council could, if they saw fit, appoint an- other person to the position. This proposition was not a proposition of his own. The committee had considered it desirable that that appointment should be held by the chairman of the committee, and if there were present that evening any members who were present at the com- mittee meeting, at which that arrangement was come to, they would bear him out in saying that he had not ' used the slightest argument to influence the committee in taking up that view. So far from that he had even said at the time, that if he did take the appointment it would be a serious addition to his many duties. He did not want either the chairmanship of the Rivers'Commit- tee, or the position of representative of the Corporation upon the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. It was wellsknown that when the committee pursued the above ' course Councillor R. T. Fairclough's firm was engaged in a serious litigazinn with the Ship Canal Company, arid the question of the interests of the town, as apart from the interests of Messrs. Fairelnugh and Sons, and the Ship Canal Company .had to be taken in hand by some- one who had no interest in either one or the other, but who preferred the interests of the town. Be (Coun- cillor Roberts) had had during the past few months as chairman of the committee a most anxious and arduous time. They had done some very difficult work for the Corporation and that to the best of their ability, and at a time when it was extremely unfortunate, they were ft without the assistance and guidance of their chair- man. He (Councillor Roberts) had had to step into the

breach, and he had done his best, and whether he had succeeded or failed was a matter for the Council and the town generally to express an opinion upon. But he was out prepared to do the work of the chairmanship of the commitree, and for the appointment in question to go out of the Man is of the chairman.. That was the plain English of tint matter. GREY said the policy of the Government was ont,i a centinuatinn of the policy of the late Government. Hon. members must form their own (mit ion as to the scope of the article of the Treaty of Berlin releva it to the point. div.head: MR. W. DIGQ.LE AND THE WARRING
div.p: MR. W. DIGQ.LE AND THE WARRING
TON FIRE BRIGADE.

A meeting was called tiy Mr. William niggle at the Cairo-street schoolroom, Warrington, at 7 30 on Monday evening, for the purpose of discussing measures to obvi- ate any difficulties in case of any fire occurring in War- , rington in the future. When 7.30 arrived, the audience , was very meagre, and Mr. niggle said that he was sorry that he had not fixed the time for eight o'clock. How- ever, to pass the time away and to give people time to get there, he would talk a little about gas until eight o'clock. Mr. Diggle then proceeded to speak about the gas in various towns, and argued that Warrington gas was very dear. In reply to a question as to whether he had got samples of the various gases, he said that he would make a sample of his questioner. At eight o'clock Mr. Diggle proceeded to give his "lecture." From be- ginning to end he was continually interrupted by hum- orous interjections which however he took in very good part. Somebody proposed that he should have a chair- man, but Mr. Diggle said that it was only lads and old Imen who wanted chairmen. He did not want one, as chairmen beck up too much of his valuable time. Proceeding with his address he said that he earne there on behalf of the firemen. His Isubject that night was a very important mae. He was deputed there by the Board of Trade to make ilinquiry into that most important matter. (Hear, hear, no, no.) He wished to show how fires could be put out better than they were now, and if he could show that, they would all agree that he was doing some good work. (Hear, hear, and applause.) A fire, as they all knew, occurred at Mr. Skelton's shop, three weeks the preced- ing Friday. At about five o'clock or a little after when the people were getting their tea ready, and filling their kettles, and the water was being used in the various works, the fire broke out and there was not sufficient water to cope with it. The reels were at Mr. Skelton's shop two minutes after the alarm. They had water playing on the shop in six minutes. In seven minutes, they had the steam up. They however had not enough firemen there to do the work, and why was that? It was because one lived at Padgate, one at Penketh, and he didn't know where. They could also not get sufficient water, and there were also too many town councillors, Arc., about. (Hear, hear and laughter.) Owing to there not having sufficient water in time, it was impos- sible to put the fire out. The Wilderspool engine which came down did its work properly because the men were trained to the work, and the Warrington men ought also to he trained. The Wilderspool men get to work at once. There were no councillors in the way, and they render, el valuable service. The build- ing was burnt down as they all knew. ("Not quite. There is somethieg left yet.'') Well they who were sober would know what he meant. (Laughter.) FP was accustomed to be laughed at. It had no effect upon him. He had a plan for getting an adequate supply of water. It had cost him a great deal of trouble to get it up. He would nropose to put a tank under the Market Hall, 20 feet by 30ft, arid six feet deep. (Suppose it " busts." arid laughter.) I'll " bust " thee if tha' does not hold noise. (Lairehter.) Proceeding Mr. Diggle said that this tank under the Market Hall would be fitted with conneetione so as to give an adequ- ate supply of wa'-er for 300 3, ards around, in face, all the centre of the town. Fr Bank Park and the Town Hall and round that district, he would have the new baths as a some,' of water supply. He next went to the Workhouse. (Laughter, and cries of " Are you going to stop there.") H 11,.peri not. To supply the water for the district round the Workhouse, he would enlarge the pond there. Mr. Diggle then proceeded to deal with other parts of the town, aod was frequently interrupted. At the close he wished to know whet hr there were any questions, hut as none were put, Mr. Lawless proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Di,..,21e for his address. Mr. Dodd seconded, hut before it was put, the audience left the room leaving Mr. Dergle tic himself, well satisfied that he had been able to expound his opini ins to a tolerable number of listeners.

At a meeting of the Ddrwen Town Council on Monday it was decided that all the public elementary schools in the borough should be closed, owing to the prevalence of measles.

On Saturday last several persons in one district of Leicester purchased tinned meat at a grocer's shop. Twenty-two persons ate some of the meat, and all after- wards beca me ill. One of them has since died, but all the others are reported to be recovering.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN DOCKS. On Monday a dock labourer, named Rafferty, was engaged at Runcorn docks M diecherging flints,when he received an injury to his leg by the tailing down of the doors of a truck. On examtniug the limb it was found that no b riles were broken. OUTBREAK OF MEASLES AT RUNCORN. Owing to an out break of measles in the town it was foaled riecsssery to close Mill Brow infants' school at the beginning of the week. The disease is of a mild type, and the benool will probably re-open on Monday. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. A sitting of this Court was held on Tuesday before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. Tne business com- prised 40 original summones ; 11 default summonses ; and 10 judgment summonses. There were no cases ot public interest. Sr. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. Mr. B. liniveton gave the lesson at the weekly meet- ing of this class on Sunday afternoon. There was a good attendance. Two solos were sung, Mr. Atherton con- tributing " Only an Armour Bearer " and Mr. S.iingler "0, what shall the harvest be." Mr. W. Once was the accr mp mist, and he also contributed two organ solos viz " Qooniam," and " Beueoictus " from Mez ores 12!..11 Mass. ORDINATION OF LOCAL CLERGYMEN. The Bishop of Ches, er held an ordination in Chester Cathedral on Sunday. The Rev. Vvvyan Henry Copley Moyle, 8.A., of Lincoln College, Oxford, licensed to All Saints, Runcorn : and the Rev. Albert Ernest Nicholas Simms B.A , of Trinity College, Danlin, licensed to Frodsham, were ordained deacons. Tee Rev. Herbert Boiseau Firth,B.A., of Lincoln College, Oxtord, and Salisbury Theological ' College, who has been at Runcorn for one year, was ordained priest. DRUNKENNESS. At Runcorn Police Court, in Tuesday morning, before Mr. E. Imison and Mr. T. Handley, a boatman named Enoch Rawlinson was charged with being drunk and disorderly in High-at. the previous night. The case was proved by P.C. Lee, and the prisoner was fined 103. and costs or in default of payment fourteen days' imprison- I ment. Be went to prison.—On Wednesday morning at the same court, hefore Mr. E a coleured sailor named Joseph Emilia was lined ss. including costs for being drunk in Duke-st. the previous night. Sergeant Lee proved the Case. INDECENCY AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. F. J. Norman and Mr. E. Imison, at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday morning, Mary Murphy, and Margaret Gibson, alias Stagg, were charged with indecent conduct the previous night. The tormer pri- soner, who was described as a complete pest and nui- sance, made her 24th appearance, and had only been liberated from gaol a few days,as ter a term of imprison- ment for stealing at Northwich. Stagg made her 20 h appearance, and hid previously been sent to prison for , similar offences. A fine of 40.. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment was imposed.—Mary Con- nolly was sent to prison for fourteen days for a similar offence. Sr. LUKE'S ANNIVERSARY SERVICES. The Rev. .1. D. Thomas, of Bolton. but formerly of Runcorn, preached the anniversary services in connec- tion with St. Luke's Congrezational Sunday school on Sunday. The morning and evening services were con- ! ducted in Bethesda Congregational Church, and there were good congregations. In the afternoon the rev. gentleman delivered an interesting address to teachers, scholars, and parents in St Luke's schoolroom. Mr • I Thomas alluded to the gc od work done in connection . with the institution for many years, it having answered las a mission, whence many other churches and schools 1 , had been benefited. They who laboured there laid an I excellent foundation on which to raise the superstruc- ture.He encouraged the teachers and officials to continue ! their praiseworthy efforts. At each service special pieces were sung by the choir and children, the latter having been efficiently trained by Mr. G. Lacy. Mr. le routeur presided at the organ. The eoll,N•tlccia realised £7l4s. FARM FIRE NEAR RUNCORN. About 10 30 on Wednesday evenirw a fire broke out at Union Farm, Dutton, belonging to Mr. William Fowles, I Messengers were despatehed for the Runcorn, Willers- pool, and Warringten fire brigades, an i all three arrived in good time. The Runcorn brigade received informa- tion shortly before twelve o'clock. They at once turned out in charge of Deputy-SuperiWendent William Wright and were the first to arrive at the term, reaching there about a quarter te one o'elork. The fire had not as- sumed very large dimensions, it being confined to a large stank of wheat straw weiehing about 30 tons. This was totally destroyed, but with the exception of a few farm implements, no further damage was done. There were four stacks of hay and a number of outbuildings but fortunately these did not become ignited. The Wilderspool and Warrington Brigades seeing their ser- vices were not required did not stay very long. The Rtincern Brigade returned home about seven o'clock. The damage is estimated at about £lOO and is covered

by in surance. • RTYNCORN AUXILIARY or TUE S.P.G. At the Episcopal churches in Runcorn,Weston,Haltnn, and Weston Point, the annual serinms on behalf of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts were preached. The preachers included the Rev. W. E. Paige, of Wellinoton, New Zoaland,in addition to the local clergy. Public meetings were held on Monday and Tuesday. At Shaw-at. echo Is on Monday evenin.r a well attended meeting was addressed by the Rev.J. D. Ozanne, vicar of Mosaics-, and at one time curate at Runcorn. The Rev. A. J. Jameson presided, and briefly introduced the speaker. Amongst those also present welt) the Rev. H. B. Firth and Mr.Pownall. Mr.Ozanne in the course of his address referred to the great and silccefill work the society was dning,and stated that if the English people folly realised the importance of missionary enterprise it would be more liberally assisted. He asked those present not only to give their money for thp support of the cause of missions hut to pray for its success. A meeting was held in the Weston Schools the same evening and crag achire9aed by the Rev. W. E. Paige, of Wellington, N,sr Z Aland. He also spoke at a meeting held in the National Schools, Run. corn. on Tuesday evening. In the absence ot the Vicar, who was unable to he present, the chair was occupied by the Be,. A. J. Jameson. The speaker in his interest- ing address spoke of what ho considered to he the ad- vantages of an Established Church. Twenty-five years ago he was in 'favour of disestablishment hut his ex- perience in the C •Inniea had le him to alter hia opinion. Be believed it was for the host cause of the church to he established.—The Rev. fl R. Mrth read a short account of what the local branch of the society had done. Votes of thanks conclurd-d the meeting. At West'm Point,the same evening.the Rev, F J. Powell, vicar of Knotty Ash, sp-ike at a meting held under the auspices of the society, in the schoolroom. TM; DROWATTAYG FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

lAt the Rurcarn P CP S'a' ion on Saturday morning, Mr. T. E. Worslea- hold an invest concerning the death of a boy named Ralph Raven iernft. who reside I with his parents at 8, Lyon-,tre-t. Hunoorn. As already re- ported the both, was piek,9l out of the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn on Friday marning.—Miry Ravens- croft was the first mitres.; Geed, and She stated that she was the wife of It alih Ravenseroft, Batman, Runcorn. She identified the body a. that of her son who waa eight years of age. About 8.30 on Monday morning she sent I him on an errand. He was onle partly dressed at the I. time. She never saw him again until his body was brought home on Friday morning. She had ne idea of what induced the child to go to the place where his body was found ; and she could not ascertain that anyone went with him. A young man named Thomas Sadler had told his mother that he saw the deceased following a band on the Halton-road on Monday.—Doorge Piekstock, 21 Collier- street, captain of the flit Herbert. stated that he found the body floating in Bridzewater Canal, near Bates Bridge at 3.15 the previous morning. He brought it to 13,3tt0m Locks and gave inform atinn to the police. Be did not know the deeeased —P.C. Gregory deposed that he received information of the finding of the body from another police offieer, about six n'el rk on Friday morn- ing. It Wag then lying at the deceased's home. He ex- amined the body and found there were four cuts on the head which appeared to have been caused by a towing boat after death. His opinion was that the boy was proceeding along the towing path to the football field when he fell into the water. The path was not particu• larly dani2erous. The jury returned a verdict of " Found Drowned."

SUDDRN DRATR OF A QUARRYMAN AT WRSTON. At the quarry of Messrs. finest, 'Wale, and King, Weston, James Percival, 63 years of age, a quarryman, who resided At Five Crosses, near Frodaham, suddenly expired whilst engaged at work on Saturday morning. He was apparently in his usual health when he com- menced work, but at about a qu seer to eight he sud- denly called out to a fellow-w-Tkman, "Oh, dear !" Tie fell to the ground and expired almost immediately. Thy deceased, who was a martir I man. had been en2aged et the quarry between 30 and 40 years.—Mr. J. E. Worsley coroner, held an inquest at the Praanect Inn, Weolton,on Tuesday morning, with referener to the death of the de- ceased, when the fActs given above were borne nut.-- Dr. McDougall stated that he ma le an examination on the body and found that death was doe to syncope or failure of the heart's action. 11. thought it VMS a very imprudent thing to do on the part of a workman, to give the deceased man water when in an unconscious condi- tion. In summing up, the Coroner referred to this matter, and eater] that a msn when unconscious was unable to swallow. But he believed the water was given the man with the hest inten-ions It would have been better if the ennstable had been summoned, for he waft a member of the st. John Ambulance Associetion. He (the Coroner) would advise workmen to attend the classes held under the auspices of ttat noble omanise- tion so that they might know how to render first aid. A verdict that death was due to " Natural Causes " was returned.—During the early s•ayes of the inquiry the Coroner commented noon the conduct of a juryman who was requested to retire. k substitute was soon afterwards found, and the inwiest proceeded.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURPAY, JUNE 15 1895!
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURPAY, JUNE 15 1895!

THE TRADE OF RUNCORN._ This: week no fewer than twenty men have been stopped'at the United Alkali Works at Runcorn. TOO number of hands employed at these works does rilt now exceed sixty. It is pleasing to note that the work at Runcorn docks is brisker than has been the case for some time past. With regard to the proposed establishment of aluminium works at Weston Point, negotiations are still in progress for the purchase of lan.j, and it is expecred that some representatives of the Company at Birmingham will visit Weston Point early next week. GIRLS FRIENDLY SOCIETY'S EXCURSION. About 250 associates and members ot the Girls' Friendly Society, Runcorn, had their annual excursion to Marbury and Great Budworth od Thursday. They embarked at B Atom Locks ane proceeded to Weston Point, and thence along the river Weaver. The day was beautifully fiae and the outing Was a most enjoyable one. Tea was partaken of at Gvat Budworth. Runcorn WAS not reached until late at nigh, the return journey occupying three hours. THE ELECTION IN NEWTOWN WARD. To-morrow (Saturday) the election of a councillor for the Newtown ward to 'fill the vacancy on the Runcorn Urban Council will take place. The candidates are Mr. Thomas Reynolds and Mr. John Jones, both residents in the ward. The polling place will be in Newtown schools Shaw-st.. and the polling station will be open from 12 noon to 8 p.m. After the dos. of the poll, the boxes will be conveyed to the Town Hall where the counting of votes will be proceed?d with. The result will pro- bably be declared about 9.30. ANOTHER FIRE NEAR RUNCORN. Ebortly after three o'cllek on Thursday afternoon in- formation was given to the Runcorn police that a lire had broken out at the Yew Tree Farm, Norton, occupied by Mr. John Henry Horton. The fire " buzzer " wag sounded and the brigade under the Deputy-superinten- dent, promptly turned out with the engine. They found on arrival that a stack was partially destroyed. The flames had got a firm hold, but favoured with a good supply of water, the firemen gained the mastery. There was destroyed 24 tons of hay, 10 tons of straw, and part of a galvanised shed, and the estimated damage is about £3OO. This is covered by insurance. The origin of the , fire is unknown. Superintendent Atherton WAS early 00 the scene, and as in the case of the fire at Dutton the same morning, rendered most valuable assistance. RUNCORN BOATING CLUB. A general meeting of the above club was held in the Cocoa Rows on Tuesday evening. The Secretary read ' several additional rules, which were—with one slight amendment—unanimously carried. Mr. J. A. Smith, junr., said that at the last meeting, as the majority pre- , sent would be aware, the posts of captain and sub- captain were only filled temporarily, with the object of ascertaining if there were any better qualified amongst the new members, and he had now pleasure in proposint that the captain and sub-captain he fiaally elected. Mr. E. H. Eniveton proposed, and Mr. E. Speakman seconded, Mr. F. Abel for the post of captain, which was agreed to; and Mr. H. Davies proposed Mr. J. H. West for the post of sub-captain, which was also unanimously carried. It was arranged that Mr. E. Speakman coach up a crew (four oar) trorn the Thursday members to compete against one from the Saturday members, and that a race be run about a month hence from the Boat- house, Rock S tvage, to Pickerings. It was resolved to leave the skiff racing over until a little later in the season. AN EXCURSIONIST'S FOOLISH FREAK. As an excursion train from Ashton-under-Lyne to North Wales was passing through Frodsham Station early on Saturday morning it was noticed by an onlooker that one of the passengers was seated on the buffers between two of the carriages, lie in- formed the railway officials of what he bad seen,and in consequence, the train was stopped at Dunham Hill. The excursionist was found to be in the posi- tion indicated, and was removed. His name and address were taken which he gave as follows Thomas Walker, Wellington-road, Ashton-under- Lyne. He was none the worse for his escapade, but he may feel thankful that be did not pay the penalty with his life.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

--- At Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, the fort- nightly meeting of the Council was held under the pre- sidency of Mr. J. Wlntyre, J.P. There were also pre- sent :—M-ssrs. J. Knowles, H. E. Fleywood, J. M. Wil- liams, J. Brandro:li, J. Weir, T. Baxter, C.C., W. Brad- ford, C. Mourifield, J. Spruce, J. D irbyshire, T. Wr.ght, S. Woodwar 1, T. Fowls, T. Darlington, J. B. Chadwick, E. Bratherton, J. Lowe, C. W. Davenport, G. Priestlier, and Mr. J. Ashton,(elerk) Mr. G. A,hron (deputy clerk), Mr. Swinton (surveyor) and Mr. J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).

and to be audited by the accountant to the District Council, or some other person appointed by them, at a remuneration decided upon by the committee. The Dis- trict Council shall have power to sell and exchange the premises on rrquest of two-thirds ot the committee, and if in the opinion of two-thirds of the Dtstrict Council the trust ought not to be continued, the Council may, with the consent of the Charity Commissioners, sell or devote the premises or the proceeds of sale to any public educa- tional purpose within the district. Sir John Brunner promised that if any organisation decided to use the premises, and the charge for the first year was more than they had been accustomM to pay, he would see that they did not lase anything. In his opinion, after the first year the charge would be very small. —lt was unanimously decided that the name of the building should be the Runcorn Guild Hall, and in de- ciding upon his, Sir John Brunner said he wished the hall to be the home of unity, concord, and mutual help- fulness ; and if there was anything in a name, he tie ught that which for centuries had been the symbol of brotherhood would be the most fitting for a hall which ' was intended, and he hoped would he fully used, as a meeting-place for those societies whose first object was the uplifting of their brethren. And iu order that it might be an incentiva for rthers to go and do likewise in some other scheme for the helping of mankind, lie would consent to the addi' ion of the words "presented by him- self "being made to the date stone. This announcement I was received with great satisfaction, and the meeting closed with a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A IDES INSURANCE AGENT.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A IDES INSURANCE AGENT.

T7i-o;;;; Wood, insurance agent, 9, Forbes-street, Stockport, rose early on Thursday morning, and ate a hearty breakfast. At nine o'clock Mrs. Wood heard screams from a closet, and going out saw her husband hanging from the roof of the closet by a clothes line. Wood was cut down,but was quite dead. He has been unemployed for some time, which preyed on his mind. He was recently an insurance agent at Widnes.

div.head: LABOUR. DISPUTE AT THE
div.p: THE LABOUR. DISPUTE AT THE
SALFORD DOCKS.

The Mediation proff.,red by the Manchester Joint Board of Conciliation in the dispute between the Ship Canal Company and the National Union of Dock Labourers has beer accepted by the labourers. Mr. G.D. the secretary to the Bard, on Thursday re- ceived a letter from Mr. T. M. Purves, the local secre- tary of the Labourers' Union, in which Mr. Purves. on behalf of the men, accepted the services of the Joint Board and agreed to attend the proposed meetinv. He added that the labourers had "no objection to any mem- ber of the Board being prtlsent.at the conference."
On Thursday evericni the Ship Canal Company sent the following reply to Mr. Kelley The Manchester Snip Canal Company. Secretary's office, 41, Spring Gardens, Manchester, 11.11 June, 1895.

Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yesterday inviting this Company to send three representatives to meet three representatives of the Dock Labourers' Union with a view to a friendly settlement of the matter to which you refer. In reply lam instructed to express to the Manchester Joint Board of Conciliation the cordi il thanks of the Company for their invitation, but as there are as many men daily offiTing their services at the ducks as can be employed a large number of whom are members of the N,tional Union), there is no necessity for the proposed conferPnce. If there were, , however, any matter requiring discussion, the Company would be very glad to avail themselves of the oppor- tunity afforded by your Board.—l am, &r:!., A. H. WHITWORTH; Secretary. Councillor G. D. Xelley.

div.head: Sul? CANAL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE Sul? CANAL AT RUNCORN.

Progress is being made with the construction of the facilities which are being provided by the Ship Canal Company for the repair of vessels at Runcorn. With regard to the proposed extension of lay-by accommoda- tion, the tender for the work has been let to Mr. Colson, contractor, of Eilesinere Port, Chester, and Frodsharn, and it is expected that the work will be commenced shortly. One of the largest ships which have been un- loaded at the Runcorn lay-by, arrived on Monday. It is a full-rigged ship ,iainerl the Sutherlandshire, and brouzlit a cargo of over 2,000 tons of wheat from San Francisco. The wheat is contained in 40,323 sacks, and these are being transhipped into barges,and takm along the Bridgewater Canal. The consignees are millers in Todmorden,Rochdale and other Lancashire towns. The captain of the vessel ;las kindly consented to allow visi- tors to inspect the vessel, and many have taken the op- portunity of doing so. Tile visitors are expected to con- tribute something towards the expenses incurred in the provision of the Sailors' Grave and Monument at Run- corn Cemetery, which Mr. W. Shaw, of the Mersey Mis- sion to Seamen, has carried out. Three large timber vessels are expected to arrive at Runcorn within the next few days.
THB VIADUCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION
CLAssus.

The statement of the income and expenditure of the Viaduct. Institute Technical Instruction Clas,..es for the 14 months ended August 31st, 1894, as submitted to the Lancashire County Council has been published. The income has been £450 178.2 d., which consists of £lBO, as grant from the County Council; £B6 10s. 61, Government grant; £6O, donation from the Newton Commissioners ; £32 164. 61, fees ; £45 45., donations to prize fund ; and sundries. The year commenced with a balance of £3B Is. 31, and the balance now at Parr's Bank is £25 9+. 4d. Among items of expenditure are £235 13s. 61, in teachers' salaries ; £l2 9s. lid., in examination fees and expenses; £3O Bs. 4d., scho- larship to Jesse Harrison; and £33 10s.maintenance salaries. EARLESTOWN TRADESMEN'S PIC-NIC.

The first annual pic-nic ot the tradesmen of Earlestown took place on Thursday, to Chester. The party numbering 107 left Earlestown by the 8.45 train, and reached Chester about 9.50. The weather was in every way auspicious, and after rambling about the ancient city, and visiting the various places of interest, including the cathedral, the party assembled at 12 o'clock at the Hop Pole restaurant where an excellent dinner was provided, and thoroughly enjoyed. A move was afterwards made to the riverside, where they embarked on board the steam launch "Ontario belonging to Messrs. Capner and Son, and proceeded up the river as far as cccleston Ferry, where they disembarked for a visit to Eaton Hall. A coule of hours was spent in an inspection of the hall, grounds, and conserva- tories and much pleasure was derived therefrom. About five o'clock they re-embarked on board the launch, and reached Chester about six, where they dispersed; each following their own inclination, in regard to spending the time remaining at their dis- posal. The homeward journey was made by the 8.35 p.m. train, Earlestown being reached at 930, after a most enjoyable day. The arrangem-ints were efficiently carried out by a committee con.ist- ing of Messrs. Attfield, Tuft, Charlton, G. Owen, •Frederick A.Brovvn (treasurer),and J. Evans (secre- tary). WRINGING MACHINRI.
