div.head: WESTON STREETS.
div.p: WESTON STREETS.

The L wal Government Board in reply to the applica- tion of th. Rural thstrict Council for an order, in then) with the plwers of the Private S'reet Works Act, 1892, in respect of certain streets at Weston, said that the Board were only willing to invest a Council with those powers as regarded streets which had been sewered, and it was not their practice to confer on a Rural authsrity the p wets to require owners or occupiers of houses to carry out works of sewerage. The District Council should therefore first carry out such works of sewerage as were required, and should then renew their application.—Mr. Aaron stated that abut fifty yards of streets required sewering. He moved that the Surveyor draw out a plan and specifica- tion for the sewering work to be done.

• WESTON WATER SUPPLY. Mr. E. Marshall, secretary of the Runcorn Urban Council, writing with reference to the complaint respect- ing the water supply at Weston, said ha a as directed by the Water Committee stating "that to make the state- ment that frequently for whole days there is no water supply at all, at Weston, is so much at variance wi,Lithe facts that they feel It should never have been made ueless you can afivln 'e something in support of it. Had you staz.ed wet a few houses in the immediate vicinity of Mr. Aaron's house were not receiving as gwod a supply as was desirable we could have understood it, as such houses are about on a level with the reservoir, but there is no warrant for going beyond that. We can say with- out hesitation that unless it is the houses referred to, there is a very fair supply at Weston, in spite of the immense inconvenience we have been put to in consequence of the continued loss of water through the great frost of three months ago. If you will give us particulars of the huuees which are not receiving a proper supply, the committee will do its best to have the matter remedied. I may say that for the past month our surveyor has been developing a plan, which if it can be carried out, will increase the pressure at Weston. Will you be good enough to submit this letter to your Authority, so that it may have equal publicity to the etatemente made at the last meeting of your Council "—Mr. Aaron complained of the incivility with which they had been treated. That morning there was not a gill of water in his house at Weston. From 9 a m. to 8.30 p.m. on the previous day they were also with- Out water.—The Chairman said the secretary admitted that there was an intermittent supply at Mr; Aaron's house.—Mr. Aaron: Yes, and at other places in Weston. The people had not had enough to wash themselves in, and some had been drinking rain water, Weston, as they knew, was a hotbed of disease, and it was largely due to the poor water supply. Mr. Farrington's report which was read a month ago showed that Weston was not properly supplied with water. On the Friday be- fore Whit Monday no house could have been better sup- plied with water, but on the following day there was practically no supply at all. The Runcorn Council made them pay for water they never got. He contended that when the water works were under private manage- ment, the water supply at Weston Was better than it was now. He considered that it was an insulting letter which had been sent by the secretary.—Mr. Ferrington on being aeked as to the supply of water at Weston said it was very intermittent. There were 101 houses with animperfect supply and he had served notices upon the , owners. On paying a visit to Weston about a fortnight ago he found about half of the houses without water.— Mr. Heywood said he would like to ask Mr. Farrington whether he considered Mr. Marshall's letter a fair state- ment of the case.—Mr. Farrington did not consider it , was so.—lt was decided that the Inspector should make his report out regarding the matter, and that it be for- warded by the Clerk to Mr. Marshall. Mr. Farrington said he would go round again previous to the letter be- ing answered.

div.head: ALLEOED STOPPAGES OF RIDUTS OF WAY.
div.p: ALLEOED STOPPAGES OF RIDUTS OF WAY.

A communication was read from Mr. William Holt, ot the Wheat Sheaf, Anti. lbw, saying his attention had been called to the hridleway leading from Knutsford- road, Antrobus, to Barber's-lane, which had been rai!ed across without leaving even a style for foot passengers. He asked what course he should adopt in the mitter.— Mr. Heywood said he understood that Townfield-dme leading from Frodsham Bridge to Frodshain had been closed to the puhlic,—lt was decided that Mr. Swinton. the surveyor, should visit the place indicated in the com- munication and report to the next meeting, and that in the latter Case mentioned by Mr. Heywood, Mr. Diggle should make ingoiries and report. THE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Farrington reported that certificates of oceupa- tion had been granted to Mr. Liti of Chnrch-st.„ War- rington, for two hotiv.s erected by him in Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath. Noisances at Walton Inferior were reported and notices were ordered to be served.

div.head: SIR T. T. BRUNNER, BART., M.P., AT
div.p: SIR T. T. BRUNNER, BART., M.P., AT
RUNCORN.
THE GUILD HALL TRUST DEED.

Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., met the representa- tives of the various trade, friendly, temperance, and musical societies of lintacnrn on Saturday afternoon, for the purpose of set' ling the terms of the trust deed of the hall which he pr Tinged to vest in the Urban District. Council for the use of the societies mentioned. The con- ference took place at the hall, which will in future he known as the Guild Hall. Mr.J.Pritchard presided,and there were al.,n present—Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk to the Council), Mr. W. Handley, who had acted for Sir John T. Brunner in the acquirement and adaptation of the hall, and a good number of representatives of local societies. At this point it may not he inappropriate to give a, few particulars respecting the all. It is built on the freehold ground previeuslv occupied by St. John's Pres- byterian Chapel and school in St. John-st. The build- logs were purchased by Sir John Brunner, and togath-r with the rec instruction and alterations which have been effected the total cost has exceeded £2,000. The chapel has been converted into an excellent assemble room, which is provi,led with a gallery and platform, and will give accommodation for between 500 or 600 persons. There are two approaches, one from St. John- at. and the other leading from the side entrance to the new hail. • An additional exit from the gallery has also been provided. It has been artistically beautified,and is admirably fitted for the purpose for which it is in- tended. Adjoining, this there is a new hall, built in the Tudor style of architecture upon the site occupied by the old schoolroom. It is two storeys high, and there is capacious cellar accommodation On the first floor there are five rooms and lavatories. One room is used as an office by Mr. Gatlev, the Secretary of the Upper Mersey Watermen's Union, who is also the caretaker. The upper stores-, which is approached by a stone staircase, forms a large and well lighted room, and is capable of accommodating shout 300 people. This will be most useful for tea meetings, &c. By an ingenious arrangement of moveable p-,rti- tions, the room can, if desired, be divided into five rooms for the purpose of committee meetings. A side entrance with gates, leads to the hall, on the opposite side of which are the caretaker's house, two club rooms, and a kitchen. Daring his visit en Saturday, Sir John Brunner inspected the premises. Be congratulated those who had had charge of its decoration on the excel- lent result of their efforts. The work had been tastefully carried out, and the arrangements were in every respect satisfactory. At the commencement of the proceedings Mr. E., Ash- ton, secretary of the local branch of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, tendered, on behalf of the trade societies of the district, congratulations and good wishes to Sir J. T Brunner on the distinguished honour conferred on liim by her Majesty. This was seconded by Mr. J. I:Milne:ton, treasurer e the Trades Conncil, and endorsed by prolonged acclamation. Sir John expressed his pleasure at receiving such an entirely unexpected reference to himself ; it had been very satisfactory .and gratifying to him to receive so many congratulations and kind wishes (haring the paAt few weeks, both from friends and from those opposed to him on political grounds. The meeting then proceeded to consider the trust deed, which after some discussion, was unanimously agreed to. The terms provide that t premises aro to he conveyed by sir John Brunner to the Urban District Council upon trust, to be used, under the management of a committee for meetings of Trades and Labourers' Unions,- Friendly or Provident Societies, and after providing for these pur- poses, by any other unions, associations, societies, fse., cr for the promotion of any religious, educational, temperaace, political, or recreative purposes. The committee is to consist of three members appointed by the Urban District Council, one of whom must be a member of that body, aril of a representative from each society, lodge, or association using the rooms and undertaking to pay the rent for one year. The committee is to be apnointed annually in January, and Is to meet monthly. The treasurer and secretary shall be elected at the first meeting of the committee in each year, and their remuneration is then ti The decided. The officers having custody of moneys are to be guaranteed; all moneys to be paid into some bank ; the premises and contents to he insored against fire ; and the committee to charge to each hotly using the premises a rent as nearly as possible In proportion to the apace and time occupied. No alcoholic liquors or intoxicating drinks to be sold, distributed, nsed. or consumed on the premises. Sir John Brunner undertake': to pay the treasurer £2O a rear for three rears. After the expiration of three rears from January Ist. 1895. the committee shall invest a sum af not less than £0 annualiv in a aenarate account aa a repair or maintenance fund, until the accumulated pay- ments amount to £260, when they may cease except so far as may he necessary to keen up the fund to that arununt. The accounts are to be made up half yearly,

div.head: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Knowles occupied the chair. There were present in addition to the members of the Runcorn Rural Council, the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gast Adi, Mr. 'P. Handley, J.P., and Mr. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. G. Ash.on (depots, clerk).

THE ACCOUNTS OF THE BOARD. It was reported that Mr. J. F. Jardiaon, public audi- tor, had audited the acc,mnts and found them correct. The balance of £2,374 164. 11. i, as shown to be in the hands of the treasurer was the same as appeared in his books.

div.head: EVILS OF STREET BETTING.
div.p: THE EVILS OF STREET BETTING.

The Clerk- of the Wolverhampton Union forwarded:a copy of resolution asking them to adopt it, and assist them in getting the Home Secretary to alter the law se as to enable local authorities to deal in a satisrictory manner with the evils of street betting. The resolution was "that this Board viewing as it does with alarm and regret the prevalence of betting and gambling in this town and neighbourhood, and 'feeling that this may he the Cause in some measure of drunkenness, and un- doubtedly is the cause of adding considerably to the amount of poverty and destitution, respectfully urges up m the local authorities comnrised in the Wolverhamp- ton Union that they should take all necessary means for the passing of by-laws, such as would check in everr possible way the practice of betting in the public streets and other places.."—Mr. Brandreth remarked that the only gambling they had at Helsby was that of lads playing marbles. • (Laughter.) Mr. Baxter, C.C., said the matter did not effect their Union very much.—Mr. Dartwahire said it was a very important subject, and they ought to give their countenance to any effort to suppress gambling. HO thought they should act upon the suggestion. They should set their faces aeainst it. —Mr. Williams said he sympathised very much with Mn Darbyshire. It was an evil which prevailed very much in their district. The other day he saw two sets of hobbledehoys playing pitch and toss at Frodsham. He would be very pleased to second any proposition that would support the Wolverhampton Union in their en- deavours.—The Clerk said the police sari power to sum- mon those they saw playing at pitch and toss.—Mr. Brandreth said it was not a question for the Guar,li ins to take up.—Mr. Woodward said he sympathised and heartily snpported the tetnarkA of Mr. Dirbyshire. He thought it was a question for them to take lip, rite evil was tilling their workhouses and was more prevalent in country places than some seemed to think. In their neighbourhoed he had heard complaints of the Sunday being spent at the road ends and in secret places by lads , playing pitch and triss.—Mr. Bratvireth said he did not ' think there was betting to any great erect in the dia. trict. As their Clerk said with respect to this Sunday betting, the police had powers, .if they would only exercise them.—Mr. Aaron asked whether the police had power to summon any persons who were naught betting or gambling on private land. A reply in the negative was given.—Mr. Handley thought they might send a letter to the Home Secretary in accordance with the terms suggested in the cotn- munieation. If they got the power, local authorities would be able to step in where the police did not do their duty.—Mr. IFleywond said it was not a matter for the Board of Guardians ; the police hart already power to • prevent any kind of betting in the public streets. There was nothing for the Board to pas or approve of. He moved that the communication be on the table.—Mr. Priestner seconded. The Rev. Canon Wood said he would like to express his satisfaction at hearing the subject taken up so well by the members. He wished to point out, that so far as he understood the reading of the Com- munication, the objet was to set local authorities to work to lessen gambling, not to alter the law or make any fresh powers, but merely to strengthen the barks of those wishing to do their dury. As the matter had been brought before them it would be a great pity if it was negatived, and it would appear as if they were in favour of ganahling.—On the matter 'icing put to the vote it was decided by 16vote5 to 3 to support the Wolverhamp- ton Board of Guardiang, by sending a letter to the Home Secretary on the matter. THE FicOD9HAM RELIEVING OFFICER'S SALk RY

Mr. Thomas Riley, relieving officer (If the Frodsham district, wrote asking for an increase of salary. He in- formed thcm that he had bnen in the scrvice inf the Union 20 years, and although the work had boen materially increased, the salary remained tlo same as when appointed, namely, 2.75. Fie pined nut the in- crease in the population ; to the number of persons receiving out-reliet ; and owing to Frodsham being on the highway between Ches'er and lAlarrington,thrre vras a large propnrtien of v:lgrants to deal with ; the number in the last two years being 2,140 He had to have a conveyance, the expense of which came to nearly a quarter of his salary. TIIP rateable value of the ,Union since 1874 had incra,:ed 40 per cent., and the popula- tion 41 per cent.—Mr. Heywood said it wuild he wise to refer the letter to the committee. He would give notice that at -the next meeting he would propose a r•solu'ion that Mr. Riley have an advanee cr otherwise as the committee deride. The committee a ppolnted was com- posed of Messrs. Aaron, Lewis, Handley, Williains, Wright, Mclntyre, Knowles, Brandreth, Baxter, Priest- ner, and Heywood.

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.

Mr. Handley reported on lochalf of the viqiting com- mittee with regurd to the provision of the men's dormitories, which had h-en pressed upon them by the Government inspector. They had got the estimate of the architect. Mr. n VIPS, of Roneorn, which showed that the cost would not exceed £l5O. It did not follow that they would spend that sum, but it was neceaslry that they should apply to the Local Government Boa td for sanction to harrow £l5O for the extension of the bedroom accommodation. He moved a resolution to that effect.

div.head: FINANCP:.
div.p: FINANCP:.

In presenting the report of the Finance Committee, Mr. FI-ywond .pointed mit that the amount required for out-relief at Frndsham was £29. whin', usually was E 35. It was the inweqt amount for out-relief for some time. This concluded the business.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, (Continued from paoe
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, (Continued from paoe
'THURSDAY.

In the House of Corn-rn—o—n-s--;;;;fi;ursday evoning Sir E. GREY, replying to Mr. KNOWLES, said Her Majosty's Ambassador at St. Petersburg had been assured by the Russian Government that a roll inquiry would be held into the murder of Mr. CRAMSHAW, and that measures were being taken by the local auth.,rities to prevent further disorders. Sir W. HARCOURT moved the resolution giving the Government all the time of the House for the remainder of the session. He said the Government proposed to set apart Fridays for the &tin-Wes and ta devote the rest of the time to the consideration of measures which they had laid on the table. With these measures it was their desire and intention to proceed, and he believed that they tnight, with fair discussion, be disposed of during the present session. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR diii not oppose the motion, and he thought that the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER was animated by an extremely sanguine spirit—that the Government had set before themselves a task which neither they nor the House could possibly perform. The House then went into committee of Supply on the Civil Service and Revenue Department Estimates. On the vote towards the grant to the imperial British East Africa Company on their retirement from Africa, Sir E. GREY explained that it ro!ated to the affairs of the country lying between Uganda and the coast. It was, he said, necessary that the enqtrni and influence of the British Government should be maintained over that ter- ritory, primarily as A means of communication with tiganda,and Her Majesty's Government had come to the conclusion that it was also necessary to construct a rail. way between Ueanda and the coast This railway would be commenced as soon as possible. The Government proposed that the country between Uganda and the coast should be included as a British pro,oetnrate. It was estimated that the cost would be £3OOOO a year. The House divided near midnight, after the closure had been accepted, and the numb-ra were—'or the v0te,249; against it, 51 ; Government, majority, 198.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOA ItD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOA ItD.

At the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, the monthly meeting of this board was held. Mr. J. Pritc- h4rd occupied the chair, and there were also present : RPv. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaidi, Dr. Mc D Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., Thomas Handley-, J.P., E. Imison, J.P., and J. Moss (, lerk).

div.head: 'INCREASE OF SALARIES.
div.p: 'INCREASE OF SALARIES.

The School. Management Committee recommended that the salaries of the following teachers be increased : —W. Kerman, to £B5 per annum ; J. C. Cragg,, to £BO per annum ; Efts ElllB3O, to £45 per annum ; "Annie Perkins, to £55 per annum.—The Clink was instructed to see that the alterations in the playground at Green- way-road School be carried out without delay, awl it was also recommended that William Oliver, age 13, be appointed monitor at Greenway-road boys' school, his duties to commence on July 15t,1895, and his wages to be at the rate of 2s. per week.—Dr. Gastaliii said he would like to know if the salaries were to be increased every year.—The Chairman stated that the members of the committee when considering the matter thought it was not very desirable to increase salaries, considering thesdepression in trade, but the teachers were fully en- titled to the advance when they took into consideration the length of service and the scale of salaries arranged by the .13 iard.—A discussion ensued in which it was point() out that no scale of salaries had been arranged by the Board, but on comparison with the salaries paid by other boards it was found that the teachers were en- titled to increases—The minutes were passed.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of committee showed that proceed- ceedings had been taken against 11 parents, that 25 had been summoned, and that 19 appeared. The visitors reports for the month ending May 24. h showed that the number of scholars on the rolls woe 3,418 against 3,478 ,in May last year. The decrease of 60 took place in the first six months, but since then the number had been stationary. The attendance was very good during the month, reaching an average percentage of 85. The aver- age attendance was 2,905 being 8 more than the corres- ponding month of last year.—The minutes were approved.

div.head: PROPOSED INCREASE OF MEMBERS,
div.p: THE PROPOSED INCREASE OF MEMBERS,

Mr. Pritchard ;gain moved that it was desirable that the numter of members be increased to 9, and that the Clerk be instructed to approach the Educatiou Depart- ment tor its sanction to such increase, to take place at the next triennial election. As the matter had been be- fore the Board since March the members had had ample time to investigate the matter and of coming to a deci- sion. The grounds upon which he moved the resolution were firstly on account of the increased duties conse- quent upon taking over the old schools and the erection of new schools, the Board becoming responsible for 600 more children. There was no disguising the fact that the duties were increasing. Then secondly nine members would he more fully representative of the ratepayers than seven, and would make a stronger Board which would be better for committee work. And, thirdly, according to the recommendations of the Edu- cetion Department, Runcorn with a population of 19,000 was entitled to nine members. There was no necessity for him to go into these points as he had already done so previously—Mr. T Fiendley seconded the proposition. —Dr. Gaetaldi thought they !Mould come to an under- standing upon the matter in a proper way, and he thought it would be better for them to resolve them- selves into cortimittee.—Mr. Taylor said the matter had been hanging on for some time now; it had been before the Board seven or eight times, and it had been adjourned on account of perhaps one or two members being away. He thought they were in a position now to come to a clecisien. He felt that it was essential for more reasons than one that they should have an increase if it was ! possible to get one. The duties were becoming heavier year by year. The committee work was heavier, and there was a difficulty in getting members to attend the Scheel Attendance Committee, and he must say that the work did fall heavily upon a few members of the Board. He was quite sure that the ratepayers would not be satisfied with seven members dealing with large amounts such as they would have to deal with. He could not see on what grounds anyone could object to the proposal at all. If it was a matter of being afraid of the result of the forthcoming election he thought it was a narrew-ininded way of looking at the question. Re had not the slightest fear in that respect, and hoped no other member on that Board had. If the ratepayers thought they could get better men to serve them let them get them.—Mr. [meson thought the matter should be dealt with now,but he did not find that public opinion had been brought to bear on the subject. The public seemed indifferent as to whether they had seven or nine members, and he did not see any great advantage in increasing the members. There was no invariable rule on the part of the Education Department respecting the number of members. He found that in one case with a population so high as 25.000, there were only seven members. The main argument for the increased number was that the present members of the Board did net attend to their duties. The remedy for that was to appoint a fresh board. So far as the Attendance Committee was concerned if they had two additional members he thought they etotila not have any better attendance there. It would be wiser if they put more of that com- mittee's work on the Clerk so that he might impair, inte the cases. There was a distinct disadvantage in having different members on the School Attendance Committee each month. If the people summoned before that com- mittee met the same men time after time it would have better effect. It was perfectly true that they were going to have increased dories, but he found that the Texteth School Board made their offiner do R. great deal of work which the memhers found was done more efficiently by him than by them. The public seemed perfectly satisfied with the present nitie.her and lie slanuld vote agai t ti. rev,- In' ion.—The Rev.Cannn Wood contended that the Board so far as its duty regarding attendance was concerned had done its duty eo well that the attendance of the Children was remark able enrel. There was not a single braneh of the Beard's work in which they could not con- era tele te t heineelves as etendine very well in comparison with other towns, and that being so they should not think of making alterations. As to saving the town would he better Tenn...anted, it was often better repre- sented by two than by 30 or 40. But they were not die- e.uesine mere the ries and it was a very unfortunate thing to make alteratinns unless absolutely necessa rr,— Dr. M Thee/all said he was in sympathy with what Canon Wood had said. He had previously spoken against the resolution and he was of the same opinint. s' ill —Mr. Taylor saiel Mr. Moos could hear him nut in Racing that wt en as many a. 30 pennle had been wait. ing to appear before the School Attendance Cnmmittep,i had been necessary to send out fora member of the Board —Mr. Handley thought it would be wise to have nine members. It would he more folly renreseastative of the town. On reference to the GoyernmPnt statistics re- garding the number of memte re it would be found that the mej eet_v of Boards had more members than Run- corn. In delegating the duties of the School Attendance Committee to the Clerk, they would be taking duties from the members who n..ght to bear them. The Clerk was there to adYiee the members,—Canne Wood said Mr Imisnn's argument Was not to put the duties of the sehool Attendance Committee on the shoulders of the Clerk,but that they would be better done by one or two members than more.—The Chairmen said that fresh work Was corning upon the Board, and it was necessary to increase the number of members. He Was of the opinion that they did violence tea the principle of representation by only haven!! -even mem- hers on the Board. On all occasions he had been im- partial to the denominational schools and seen equal justice on every necasien.—Dr. McDougall hoped the chairman would steer clear of any statements of that description. He Was opening an element of discussion which Was infinitely better left nut. Personally he had never known a representatives of the School Board do other than discharge hie duties in a straightforward rnanner.—Onntinuing. the Chairman said his desire was to make the schools as efficient an educational inatrai- ment as possible, and in hit; opinion twe more members would give strength to the Board—Dr. McDougall thought it was necessary for him to eeplain why he de- clined to he ran the School Attendance Committee. A VIOLENT PRISONER—MAD THROUGH DRINK. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Borough Police Court P. illiarn Darnell, 12 Stanley-street, saddler, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Friar's Green at 8.10 on Thursday night ; he was further charged with assaulting P.C. Hollingsworth, and also I charged with stealing a half-pMt glass value 3d. from the "Higher Seven Stars," Bridge-street.—The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner came to Warrington on Tuesday last, and on Thoraday evening he went , several times to the " Higher Seven Stars" vaults, in a , state of intoxication and was refused any liquor. At 7 O'clock he went again and while the barman was turned sway he took two glasses and put them in his pocket and walked away. Pr. Hollingsworth was informed and followed him into Friar's Green where he found prisoner with his coat off and waritins: to &lilt anyone. One • glass was found in his rp.cket and Hollingsworth in arresting the defendant was bravely assisted by head bailiff Lewis and bailff Knight who were passing.— John B- .ton, barman at the vaults proved the theft, and added that the other glass was fcund (in the floor.—Constahle Hollingsworth slated that he found the prisoner stripped to ids shirt and trousers and -behaving like a madman. Witness took him to bis lodgings but prisoner became very violent indeed and fought li.ke a maniac. He was hrougkt down to the :Police Station with the assistance named. Prisoner there stata-d that he had rinli jist crime out of Kuutsford Gaol for as,,aniting the police at Runcorn.—Mr. Lewis, in corrohoeating the last witness' statement, said that it took four them to hold nriFnmer, who in his struggles actually kicked himself naked. FIH endeavoured to kick them in a viral part and hut for his having no boots on be would ti ye hurt them severely. According to the asitnes es' eraohic statement prisoner "drew himselr up and ki.:..ked like a horse."—li Court prisoner appeared -very weak and ill from his previous night's debauch. He said he was very sorry and did not recollect taking the glass. Drink always made him mad.—Alderman Harrison said prisoner had attempted to commit a very serious offmce and he wenld have to go to goal for 14 days for the assault and have a conviction recorded against him for the theft. On going down to the cells prisoner almost fell down the ste pa from illness and for Some time after cnild be heard groaning in pain and suffering from the " hhies," THEFT OF A Pin's HEAD. At the Borough Police Court-, Warrington, on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, William fligg;ns, 7. Smith-street, was charged with stealing from the shop door of Joseph Shaw, Bridge—lreet, a pig's head, value 44 8-1., on S.tnrlac night.—Mr. Hunt said that prisoner was a briekas, ter's labourer and on Satur- day nitt after 11 o'clock. Thomas Wools, employed in shrip, saw the prisoner pass the shop a number of times in a suspicious manner and at length noticod him step on the doar-sten and take a pig's head off the hooka good heizhst up. Prisoner put it under his coat as well as he wag able and then disappeared down Dolman's-lane. Sergeant Chantler who was close by was irnmedietly informed and in comnany with Woods they follawed the prisoner to Smith-street, off Mersey-street. Green's-court, a young man with a black character, was charge -1 with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-street, on Sunday afternoon and with assaulting Mary Robin- on at the same time and place.—Mary Robinson, whose left ey.; was badly discoloured and cut, said that the de- fendant stopped an oil man who was bringing beer to her house. She asked him what right he had to do it and defendant "up with his fist and thumped into her as if she was a big strong man." She fell to the ground , and he kicked her while there.—P.C. Bell proved arrest- ing the defendant in a drunken condition and also said that he saw him in the act of striking the complainant. —The Mayor said the Bench were determined to put a stop to this kicking and defendant would be sent to gaol tor one month's hard labour. Coop,r stated that at five o'clock on Thursday morning he was ha Marshhouse- lane, near Orford Barracks,and saw the defendant com- ing from the direction of Padgate with his pockets bulg- ing out. Witness stopped him and seirched his clothes finding 29 nets and a sack with two ferrets. His trousers were wet and the pegs of the nets damp,while there was rabbit fur among the cordage. Defendant denied any offence,and said that he had been sent for to catch some rats.—The Bench confiscated the nets and dismissed the defendant, giving him the henefit of the doubt. Clough said that he found the defendant in Town's End drunk and imbued with a desire to fight each and every one present.—A man here rushed in to Court excitedly and going to prisoner said" Did I want to fight with you Tom." GAMBLING BY YOUTHS IN A REFRESHMRNT HOUSE.— Edward Holloway, refreshment house keeper, Devon- shire Square, Runcorn, was charged with allowing gaming to take place on his premises on the Ist June. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Speeehley, Inland Revenue Officer tor Runcorn, gave evidenc- as to the defendant being a licensed refreshment house keeper.— P.S. Lee stated that about ten p.m. on Saturda‘ he was on duty in High-st., and he receivr-d a COTI4 ;Sint that a number of boys nightly went to the defendant's house for the purpose of gambling. In company with Con- stables Lee and Gregory he visited the premises at wlmloh fried fish and chipped potatoes were sold, and on going into one room he found nine youths playing cards. When he entered they were inst dealing the cards out. Two of the youths were quarrelling about the result of the previous game. Witness got hold of the pack of cards produced. and these which had been given out were thrown under the table by the youths. In the presence of a young woman who was in the shop they admitted having been in the room about two hours, and had been playing at "brag "for a half-penny a game. Witness asked whether any of them had won anything to which a youth named James Dutton (18). replied that he had lost 4d.; Thomas Wood (13) stated that he had neither won nor lost: John Ball (17) that he had lost 10.; William Faulkner (18) that he had won 41.: John Findlow (181 that he had neither won nor lost ; J )senh Wakefield (17) that he had won 21. ; Thomas Riley (18) that he had lost 4d., and Thomas and Harry IFlarrnp, aged 14 and 18 respectively, denied p'aying and Ball admitted holding the stakes. tNitnesa told the defendant's wife what the lads had said and she stated that he had told them not to play —P.O 's Gregory and Lee gave corroborative evidence, the latter stating that the young woman in the shop could have heard that the boys were gambling as they were qoarrelline about the money.— fhe defendant stated that he was not on the premises when the police came. He had stnpped the lads when he had known them to be playing tor money. His wife had also stopped them; and they had also had to turn the gas out to make them leave the premises. The magistrates considered the case proved and imposed a fine of 20s. and 18a. Bd. costa, or in default of payment one month's imprisonment.—The nine lads whose names had already been given, were then placed in the dock and charged with aiding and ahetting in the offence. An pleaded guilty with the exception of Thomas and Harry Barron. Sergeant Lee stated that he saw Thomas Flarrop go to one of the lads and ask for his money hack —Miriam Clarke gave evidence on behalf of limy Flarrop.—As there was a doubt with rerard to the charge against this latter defendant the magistrates diqtharged him, but the other defendants were fired the costs of the summon!). DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—FIenry Conk, Robert-street; was sentenced to faurteen days' hard labour, without the option of a fine, for tieing drunk and disorderly in Chnreh.st., on the 6th June. AN UNMUZZLRD Don.—William Sadler, Church-st.., was summoned for allowing a dog to be at large nnmuzzled in High-at., on the Bth June.—He was fined ss. includ- ing. costs. , BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WIFE. —Evan Roberts, mate of the smack Esther, of Beaumsris, was charged with assaulting his wife Harriet Roberta,at Rirworn, on the sth Jene. Defendant pleaded not guilty. The complain- ant stated that she had lived senarate from her husband for two years, and lived at 18, Thomas-st. On Wednes- day afternoon he tried to gain admission to the house, and threatened to take her life. At a (patter to seven he again came to the house, and forced the door open He struck witness a violent blow on the head with a clock weight which he had in his hand. Her father came to her assistance and he was also struck on the head with the same instrument. She admitted hitting the defendant with a stick in self-defence. Her head Ned profusely,and she had to go to a doctor. Sh- asked for a separation order. Mr. R. Fleatlev, father of the com- plainant, and Elizabeth lieclgecnck, gave corroborative evidence. The defendant stated that be went to the house to get some of his furniture. He displaced a wound on his head whieh, he stated, the complainant had inflicted.—A fine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days' hard labour was imposed. A separation order was also granted.

Charles Rimmer, a fishmonger, was fined 40s. and costs for having one 2,b., one 11b., an.i one lib. weight, which were unjust. This defendant had also been pre- viously convicted. RIDING d. SOUSE ON THE FOOTPATFL—George Way- well was charged with riding a horse on the footpath at Winwick on May 12th. 'Mr. R. Stuart defended. Thomas Smith said that on the above date he was walk- ing from Winwick near Hermitage, when he saw the de- fendent riding on the footpath on horseback. Witness beckoned to him to move off, but he refused and "put his heel into the horse," and witness had to move out of the road. Witness hit the horse with a stick as it went past him. In reply to Mr. Stuart, he denied hitting the defendant on the kg with the stick. Another witness named Joseph Shaw also gave evidence to seeing de- fendant riding on the footpath.—Mr. Stuart for the defence did not deny that the horse was on the footpath but urged that the defendant was causing no disturb- ance. nor annQying anybody. He was on the foetpath because his horse had lost a shoe, and he wished to ease it. A witness named Pea ire was called who supported' the statement that the horse had lost a shoe. 'fhe magistrates inflicted a fine of 2. 61 and costs. Arising out a this case, another case wa heard in which Thomas Smith was charged with assaulting George Way- well at the same time and place. Mr. Stuart said that Mr. Smith was summoned f..,r hitting Mr. Waywell on the leg as the latter passed him on horseback. He also gave the horse a severe blow which caused it to swerve and which also left a mark upon it.—The defendant denied that he hit Waywell at all, but admitted striking the horse, which he said was in self-defence. The Bench dismissed the case, Find said that they considered that Mr. Smith was quite entitled. to keep the horse off him when going on the footpath. In fact he was acting for the benefit of the public.

div.head: IMITATION-'ERE INSIXCEREST
div.p: IMITATION-'ERE INSIXCEREST
FORM OF FRAUD.

Where imitation or mimicry goes no further than fair play, there is something to be said in its defence. It argues a certain humility of mind that a person should acknowledge himself incapable of originality, and it is better to follow humbly a beaten track than to do nothing. In some other ways, however, imitation is an unpardonable crime. Where some great discovery has benefited thousands of people, and is being sought after by all on the account, it is a cruel swindle for anyon- ignorant of the true discovery to foist upon unsuspecting people something resembling it in name or outward show, but worthless in comparison with the true inven- tion. Of course the worse example of fraudulent imita tioo in this sense is the fabricating of pretended medi- cines, useless in themselves, on the strength of a super- ficial resemblance to a known remedy. Such imitators literally juggle with life and death. This journal has, in common with all the newspapers of this part of the country, published during the last two years a number of remarkable cases, in which apparently dying persons have been cured by the dis- covery published under the name of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and a large number of persons suffering from various disorders have sought the same remedy. Advantage has, unfortunately, been taken o this demand to play upon the innocence of the suffererss by offering a substitute for Dr.Williams' Pink Pills. It is important that the futility of such imitations should be publicly known. Any retailer or detailer who pretends to have "the same thing" as Dr. Williams' Pink Pills is trying to cheat the customer. Anyone who tries to sell Dr. Williams' Pink Pills loose or in bulk is trying to sell a worthless thing under false pre tences. The genuine Pills are never sold in that way. Anyone who says he can prepare the formula himself says what is not truer-no one ran possibly know what is In Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, or divine the new curative principle that they contain. Not long since a so-called analysis of Dr. Williams' WAS published—it was an ab- solute failures and entirely failed to show the comp. si- tion of this important remedy. Another point is that " cheaper" substitutes for Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are a self-confessed fraud. There Is no subsitute at any price ; but in no event could Dr. Williams' formula be sold cheap. The composition does not admit of it. But the price at which Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are sold, and their extraordinary curative effects, make the cost very low indeed compared with other remedies or medical treatment. As a final word the public should be warned against the statement sometimes made that Dr. Williams' Pir:k Pills are identical with the well-known French Pharma- copoeia remedy, Bland's Pills. Anyone who says so manifests the most ludicrous ignorance of the very ele- ments of pharmacy, and the public will be well-advised not to run the risk of buying medicine in any form from a self-confessed incompetent. When any difficulty is experienced in obtaining Dr.Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, in wooden tube, with pink wrapper and the full name printed in' red ink outside and in ; or wherever doubt is felt as to the genuineness of the goods supplied, the public are invited to apply direct to Dr. Williams' Medicine Co., 48, Holborn Viaduct, Issmion, E.C., for supplies, which will be sent post free at 2s. 9d. a box,or six boxes for 13s. 9J.

EARLESTOWN.—This local fixture which always excited considerable interest because of the aecient rivalry between the clubs, was played on the Newton ground on Saturday in beautiful weather. There was a good assembly of spectators. The Earlestown eleven went to the wickets first, the pitch being all in favour of the batsmen. Dennis and EmmAt took first place, Mills and Bates taking up the attack. With the score at 14 Emmett after contribut- ing three was clean bowled by Mills. Miller took his place, and played with extreme caution evidently feel- ing his way before attempting to score. Dennis how- ever, hit out and although for several overs the score rose very slowly, Miller finally felt secure and opening out hit Bites all over the ground, serving Mills with like contempt. Cooke went on vice Bates and with his second delivery spread-eagled Dennis' stumps, after a creaditable 28. Nokes partnere.] Miller who eontinued to make tremendous hits, and the score went up chiefly owing to the extremely bad fielding on the part of the Newton men. Boundaries came in quick succession from both batsmen. As a severance could not be effected Hindley took the ball from Mills, and bowlec a maiden over as an opening. In the next over, Nokes was a trifle late and Cooke removed his bails, his contribution being 14, and the total score 84 for three. Ball filled the vacancy and after a single and a boundary he skied the ball and was dismissed. Crow ther replaced him and with Miller dealt with the deliveries of Hindley and Cooke in an easy manner. Bates went on again vice Hindley and soon after Miller completed his half century. With the score at 130 Crowther was sent hack to the pavilion by Cooke, after adding 12.—Clare was next in and Miller gave Brierley a chance which he failed to hold. Alter a coupe of overs Clare was cleverly caught by hindlev, and Huddleston who replaced him after getting his first deliverly off Cooke to the boundary was smartly taken by Innen. Miller still continued to hit out strongly, and WAS j'Aried by Alderson who after adding 3, was caught at nud-wicket by Cooke—seers 147. Sanders replaced Alderson, and after playing carefully for some time was dismissed by Cook. Mitchell filled the vacancy and lifted Cooke for 3, Miller driving Bates all over the place. At 170 Ville went OR vice Bates and at 175, the Earlestown Captain closed his innings for 9 wickets down. Miller's contri- bution was 72. After the usual interval Newton sent in Cooke and Turton to face the bowling of Bell and Fluddleston. The two first overs were unpro luctivi, but in the third Cooke got sell away to thi boundary, and Tinton followed suit. With the score at 10 Cooke fell a victim to Bell. Mills replaced him. Several singles en- sued, ;Led after Mills had driven Hu -Idleston to the boun- dary, he was sent to the right-about after adding 11. Bates partnered Tatum, who appeared to have got set and beth batsmen hit out freely, several boundaries Following in quick succession. With 40 up, Clare re- piaeed P. 11, and after several overs, Bates w ia caught by Miller ie the slips, his contribution being 16. Hindley p3sto red 'Cotton, and was smartly caught by Clare at his first attempt. Lister filled the vacancy but was die- msed hy Iluddlestoo without scoring. Parkes partnered Tinton and together they increased the score rapidly. S, veral ehanges of bowling were made,until just on time, when Turtort was bowled by Emmett after contributing 43. The match ended in a draw, the Newton score being 109 for 6 wickets Score:—

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
PRIMITIVE METFIODIST CHURCH.

The Sunday School Anniversary services in connection with the ahove place of worship were held on Sunday when special sermons were preached, mrorning and even-., ing, hy the Rev. D. T. Maylott, of S,ockp )rt. His text ' for the morning's discourse was "Chat I may know Him and the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings, being made conformable unto His death." The two sermons were of a very interesting , character, the large congregations :it each service mani- festing great interest in them. In the afternoon a service I of song, entitled " Little Abe," was rendered in an ad- mirable manner by the choir, urvier the conductorship' of Mr. A. Spruce, who gave a solo. Miss A. Shaw also sang a solo. Connective readings were given by Mr. A. E. Calvert, of Widnes. To augment the school funds a public tea meeting was held in the Church schoolroom on Monday evening, when there was a large attendance. An excellent repast was provided, the trays having been kindly given by the friends of the scholars. The iAdies r.residiog over the table were Mesdames How- 1-Inds, Kirkland, Throssell, Allman, and Bridge An adjournment was then made to the Church where the tneeting was held, and presided over by Mr. J. T. Row- lands, of Stockton Heath. At the commencement the CHAIRMAN said that as a new corner amongst them he hoped his. services would be of great value. He had great sympathy with their work. Be believed in Primitive Methodists being true to their connexion, wherever their lots were cast. He also believed that Warrington was as susceptible to Methodist influences, and especially to Primitive Metho- dist influences seamy other part of the country. A fur- ther belief of his was that of sympathetic policy being extended to the poor as well as to the rich. Th. Rev. W. R. KIRKLAND, afterwards gave a finan- cial summary of the proceeds, which amounted to ever £25. A notable feature on the programme was the pre- sentation of Bibles from the scholars and officials to 51 185 E. J. Parka and Mr. J. R. Parks, brother and sister,who left Warrington for India on Wednesday. In presenting the Bible to Mr. John Parks, Mr. RlG- *mom, superintendent of the Sunday school, remarked that the two young people had been lifelong scholars and had been of greatservice, John having played the har- monium. Although the departure would be a great lass to them, it was hoped that it would be a great gain to the church in India. (Hear, hear.) Mr. TITCHETT presented the Bible to Miss Parks and I delivered a short address.

Mr. J. BISSELL supported the complimentary remarks made by Messrs. Higginson and Titchett. The addresses were interspersed with songs and reeitatiops,&c.. which were rendered in a very creditable manner, Mr. Stanley Bridge being the accompanist. The Rev. W. H. KIRKLAND proposed a general vote cf thanks to the donors, singers and other helpers. . _
This was seconded by Mr. FTIGOINSON and carried, bringing a very enjoyable evening to a close.

div.head: STOCKToN HEATH.
div.p: STOCKToN HEATH.

THE PAROCHIAL COIVIMITTEE'S MEETING.—The Apple- ton Parochial Committee met at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, on Friday. Mr. H. Eyes occupied the chair, and there were also present :—Messrs. J. Vk hit- low, Pearson, Coppock. J. Darbyshire' Hedgecock, Ash- ton, Hayes, and Davenport ; Mr. Ashton (clerk), and Mr.Farrington (inspector of nuisances). The Clerk read a letter from Mr. James ilepherd, Stockton Lodge, near Warrington,in which he called attention to the fact that the swing bridge at Stockton Heath (Twenty Steps Bridge) was kept open at 9.15 on the 28th inst., much over the prescribed time of thirteen minutes. He stated that the bridge was becoming a great nuisance to resi- dents on the Cheshire side of the canal, and he had him- self missed one train and been greatly inconvenienced on several occasions by it. He trusted that the matter would be brought forward with a view to proceedings being taken. This he thought was the only way to rectify the nuisance.—The Clerk produced the Manchester Ship Canal Act, section 88, which provided " Swing Bridges shall be made to tarn by hydraulic power in not more than one minute and a half of time, and shall not be kept open at any one time for any longer period than ten minutes under a penalty of not less than 403. and not exceeding £5 for every occasion on whizh any such bridge is kept open beyond such time."—lt was resolved that the Clerk write to the Ship Canal Company calling their attention to the letter from Mr. Hepherd, and also to the sub-section of the Act, and inform them that the committee would have no alternative but to cause pro- ceedings to be instituted if the bridge was again kept open longer than the prescribed time.—On the motion of Mr. Davenport, twoonded by Mr. Pearson, it was decided that Messrs. Davenport, Hedgecock, Ashton Hayes, Whitlow, and Richardson, be appointed a building committee to. whom plans of new houses might be submitted. The minutes were ap- proved of at the meeting of the Runcqrn Rural Conned at its meeting on Tuesday. Referring to the Ship Canal bridge nuisance at Stockton Heath, Mr. Baxter, CO., stated that a short time ago, when a very large vessel was proceeding up the canal the bridge at Stockton Heath was turned for over a quarter of an hour. He read afterwards that it tonk the vessel 36 hours to go from Eastham to Manchester. The vessel was certainly not going more than a mile an hour and they turned the bridge at Stockton Heath when it reached Tom Paine's Bridge. He thought it was most unreasonable for peo- ple to wait over qearter of an hour.

IT WAS MOTHER WHO THOUGHT OF IT. Many years ago there was a popular song that was in everybody's mouth. I don't remember the name of but one verse ran this way : What is home without smother? Whet nre all the j ivs we meet W hen her loving smile no longer Greets the coming of our feet P" How pathetic and suggestive it is. Even some grey- bearded old chaps can't let their minds linger on that Idea without having their eyes, spring a leak. And no shame to them either. The dear woman may be under the sod long ago but we shall never forget—there ! I can't write any more on that line myself. But here was nobody like her and never will be. We beg to introduce a young mae—God bless him ! who tells how it was that he got well through something his mother thought of. lie says that one day in March 1892, while at Dunningtan Gardens (Reading), he was suddenly seized with a pain in the left side, so great that it fairly doubled him up. Ile broke out into a perspira- tion and trembled from head to foot. nen be got home the people sent for a doctor, who at first said it was influenza and afterwards that it was pleurisy and inflammation of the bowels. The young man was put to bed and poulticed, and was so bad his wife had to Bit with him night and day. After treating him some time the doctor said to the patient's mother, "I don't think there is any chance of your son's recovering." His relatives and all who came to see him agreed with the doctor. Ile became so feeble that for five weeks he never Once set foat on the ground. Finding that the doctor's medicine was doing no gond, his mother bethought her of a preparation which th-, husband and father had used with wonderful benefit for his liver and kidneys. She gave her son some of it, ard made him keep on taking it. In three days he felt better, and by-and-bye the pain left him and he could eat and die est his food. From that hour all was plain sailing the storm was over. He gained strength daily, but it was some time before he was as goad as new. The disease had almost made a wreck of him, but in ten weeks he got back to work a well man, and has since been strong as ever. He now does any kind of work and can eat anything. "Nothing comes amiss," be says. But we are getting a bit ahead of the story. Before the attack in Dunnington Gardens he had not felt him- self for quite a while. He felt tired,languid, and out of condition. He had a foul taste in his mouth, a slime on the tongue and teeth, pain in the breast, tightness around the chest and sides, and his bowels were con- stipated, hard and swollen. Then came the attack la the Gardens. In ending his letter he says :—" The medicine that saved me was Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. It I had not taken that I believe I should have soon made my way to the graveyard, and I should like others te know what it did for me. Yours truly (Signed)WALTER HATTON, 13. Oxford-street, Caversham, Reading, Octo- ber 28th, 1892." Yes, and if Mr. Hatton's mother hadn't thought of the Syrup probably he would never have taken it. So, under Providence, he owes his life to two good women, his own mother and Mother Seigel, who also had chil- dren and gave them the same loving care that other mothers do. At the bottom of the whole :trouble was that same old mischief-maker and death-dealer, indigestion and dyspepsia, which we all hove to keep on fighting with Mother Seigel to help us win the battle.

WARRINGTON AND TILE
GENERAL ELECTION. MR. A. H. CROF•FIELD INVITP,:D TO BE THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

A meeting of the Warrington Lib3ral executive was held at the Liberal Club last night when all the leaders of the party were present. After a lengthy meeting it was unanimously decided to invite Mr. Arthur If. Cro,ft,dd to contest che borough at the next General Election. The general feeling of the meeting was that Mr. Cro•lield was the right man to contest the b )rough s L,beral candidate, and that gentleman, who was present, promised to take time to consider the matter.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
A NEW ORGAN FOR PARR HALL.

We understand that the Committee of the War- rington Musical Society have decided to build and erect a grand new organ in the new Parr Hall in time for the opening ceremony on the 26th Sep- tember next. This course has been decided upon in deference to the strongly expressed wish of Mr. J. Charlton Parr that such an instrument should if possible be placed in the Hall by the date named, thus completing the building by filling the organ chamber which would otherwise present a very conspicuous void. The new instrument will be in every respect worthy of the fine concert hall in which it is intended to occupy a prominent and permanent place, and it will, we understand, have incorporated in its interior such pipes and mechanism of the old Public Hall organ—which i; will be remembered the Musical Society has still in its possession—as the makers Messrs. (iray and Davidson can utiliso with advantage. The new organ will combine all the latest improve- ments in mechanism and stops and will be in every respect up to date. The organ front will also be of an imposing character, and the decorations such as will render the instrument ornamental as well as useful. In connection with the two concerts which are intended to inaugurate the opening of the hall we are pleased to be able to announce that the arrange- ments have been completed whereby the services of a quartet of vocalists of the I,ighest eminence have been seeured. The names of these are : Miss Anna Williams, Miss Clara Butt, Mr. Edward Lloyd and Mr. Andrew Black.
WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT

div.head: OHMY'S CIRCUS, WARRINGTON.
div.p: OHMY'S CIRCUS, WARRINGTON.
BENEFIT OF MR. OH MY.

Notwithstanding the great success which has attended the production of each programmo at the circus during the season, Monday night's benefit tor Mr. 0 imy, established a record both in " house " and selection of item,. Every seat was occupied and all the avenues of entrance were crowded with spectatms preferring to stand rather than miss the tun. In the reserved por- tion of the building was a large number of ladies, and also not an inconsiderable representation of the Town Council. - . -

A commencement was made, as usual, by the band, under Mr. Metcall's directorship, playing the overture, following which Miss Ada gave her clever exhibition of horsemanship, an amusing side to which was lent by four clowns. Alter a comic act Mr. Olimy's two per- forming ponies were'' put through their facings," and next the Brothers Elton gave an expert ring pert orin- mice. Other items which have hern previously derailed were given ; Mons. Clifton makes his appearance in evening dress, and while riding on horseback imperson- ates by changes of clothing, wigs, etc., the following Characters or scenes : Lame beggar, struggle with the police, secured in handcuffs, convict at work with the pick, and, finally, a gladiator. The clown and his rid- ! fug lion (the stage sort) were overlooked in the ring by Mr. F. J. Dell, of Warrington, who made a fairly cfpable ring-master. A creditable exhibition of 'agility was given by the Elton brothers on three horizontal bars, ! and they were succeeded by Mr. C. Hernandez whose strikingly handsome horse performs in the ring without any encouragement in the shape of a whip. 'rids :srlasal is also the cleverest jumper which has yet visited the circus, and his leap over an erection of about 51t. Bfn. wins for him a loud burst of applause. Some smart riding was displayed by Donbavand, on whose exit a tight wire is drawn across the ring. Upon this,Lest er, though only a youth, displays balancing powers which surprise the audience, whose applause is soon forth- coming. A fund of amusement was provided by a wire walking contest, which was undertaken by members of the audience and won by one aspirant who was bold enough to try in bare feet. Leo and Lester j.. Med in the production of a lecture on " The New Woman," and Mons. Clifton showed a capable performance of horse- back bar jumping. Biding, gymnastic, and jumping contests were entered Into, and Cinderella, the now popular children's pantomime was produced with suc- cess. Mr. Ohmy gave his sensational gymnastic per- formance, aed was accorded an ovation of applause such as can only be heard by a visit to the circus. Mr. ()limy, after receiving a handsome bouquet, re- turned thanks to the audience for their presence, and said that though this was the worst we, k in the year for spending money, it was more than gratifying to him to find that he had so many friends in Warrington to rally round him on this occasion. (Hear, hear.) He assured them that he had tried his best to please everyone, and he thought he had met with a fitting reward in that en- couragetnent which he tried to deserve. He would always look upon Warrington as the place where he had met with the most friends in the shortest stay of his life. This was their last week among them in Warrington and from here they were going to Douglas, 14Ie of Man, from whence they hoped to return about September,and he then hoped and trusted that by bringing the best talent he would secure their esteem, and he further hoped that now as they knew him they would continue to have the confidence which they gave him as an entire stranger. (Loud applause.) The same programme was continued throughout the week.

div.head: lattero to tin ellitore
div.p: lattero to tin ellitore

----- RINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND THE PROPOSED WHARF. Sir,—Referring to the vote of the Warrington Town Council, concerning the proposed new wharf on the River Mersey, which the Rivers Committee have twice recommended the Council to lease to us, we wish to say that, as long ago as November 1894, we obtained the consent of the Mersey Conservancy to the wharf, and in December. 1894. we obtained the consent of the Duchy el Lancaster, to sell the foreshore. In that month we entered into negotiations woh the Town Clerk, that the Warrington, Corporation should boy the foreshore and let it to us. This the Rivers Committee decided to do, and we then wrote to the Duchy of Lancaster asking them to sell all Her Majesty's rights and interests (except the right of minerals) in the foreshore to the Warrington Corporation. The Duchy of Lancaster agreed to this and the foreshore was sold for £4O to the Corporation. The Council by their v .to now say, that " they Aught to retain it for their own benefit" and not be parties to introducing competition with the Canal. Surel vthis action of the Corporation was not fully considered. We introduced the businvss of buying the foreshore from the Duchy of Lancaster to the Corpnra-i on. The Corp.7ratiou , through tii,Jr Rivers Committee, enter into terms with us, buy the foreshore, and now say "they ought to retain it for their own benefit." This after eight months of negotiations on nor part with four important Corpora. tions, preparing plans for the Duchy of Lancaster, journeys to London, Liverpool and Manchester and other

expenses. We may say in conclusion that the Manchester Ship Canal Ciimpany have given an unqualified consent in writing 'o 'he wharf being erected, s that we bay obtained the consent of the Mersey Conservancy, Duchy of Lancasbir, Manchester Ship Canal Company, and the Rivers Committee, and the Corporation now propose to retain the foreshore for their own benefit. Before taking the vote on Tuesday, we feel certain that the members of the Council who voted for the amendmimt could not lave been aware of the transac- tions that had taken pLice, otherwise surely the amsnd ment would never have been carried. We are sati-Ilsd that when the msnitiera of the Council are acquainted with all the facts of the case, we can with complete con- fidence allr‘vr our case to remain in their hands for fueter cousideration.—We are, your obedient servants,

W. A. BISHOP AND COMPA.NY. Dial Mips. Warrington, June 13, 1895.T11Ti , DARESBUItY PARISH MIMING ASSOCIATION. Sir,—The late proceedings of the above society have coma befrre the publii: in a somewhat one-sided way,and perhaps you will allow me P. state the unsectarian side of the disputes. I use the word "unsectarian" advisedly as it is a matter of sectarianism versus unsectarianism. That has divided the association. When the society was first formed it was decided it should be unssctarian' and subscriptions were received from Churchmen and Non- cornformia's alike on this understanding. The rule passed to the above effect was as follows : " That this movement be entirely unsectarian and that this be clearly stated in the rules." Notwithstanding, this, the richer church members of the Committee, headed by the Vicar, have all along, hut more particularly lately, tried to carry on the association on sectarian lines, while pro- feseedly unsectatian. To this end the nurse lately gemi- nated try that party Was elected but by means both un- constitutional and irregular. This nomination was however accepted by the unsectarian party with a de- termination to work loyally with the elected nurse. !" A special general subscribers, meeting was next held on 03rh April when a rule was passed making the Vicar fx-ofEci4 president, also one evidently intended to oust the secretary (who is ot the unarctarian party) from the position she has held so worthily for the last six years ; as also another, !placing the election of future nurses in the hands of the Executive Committee instead of in these of the subscribers generally. Further as showing the sins of the sectarian party to make the association as exclu- sive as possible, a rule was attempted to be passed to the affect, that no member should have a vote unless subscib- ing £l. or mnre. On the lat June came the annual general meeting. At this the attendance Was certainly meagre on the part of the un.ectarian because they were hopeless of carrying any broad-minded resolution, whilst of the sectarian party the members, I understand, had been requested to absent themselves, an arrangement haying been come ta amenget themselves by which the largest subscriber, had placed their resignations in the hands of the Chairman (the Vicar), and who, on the Monday following. viz., the 3rd inst., held a meeting of their own, at which as can be seen by their report it has been ! determined to start an ass,ciation of their own under I the title of the 'Vicar of Dareebury's Nursing Fund" to he worked by the Vicar, as secretary and treasurer, and by six ladies to be nominated by him, taking over the present nurse—who has been encouraged to leave the original association—in their favour. As the sectarian members of the Committee have sent in their reeignations, the unsectarian portion consisting of both Churchmsn and Noneonformists, trust to con- tinue the society under ite old title of the " Daresbury Parish Nursing Association," and on lines even broader than heretofore, encouraging all classes to subscribe what they can afford. all to have a say in the manage- ment through the Execative Committee tieing token from all classes, and elected by all the subscribers, by this means implanting an independent and self-helpful feelina in the commanitv and so counteractin-t the pauper:zing elect such an institution would produce in the parist if carried out on the lines proposed by the new departure of the" Vicar of Daresbury's Nursing Fund," —Yours truly,

Another defeat fell to—t-C;;l—o—t--of Warrington on Satur- day, and they had to submit to the superior prowess of Liverpcol. They clid nct rise to the occasion as they did against Manchester and thus they have still to look for- ward in the future for their second victory. Liverpool had a strong team as among them were D. Q. S•zeele, E. Raper, and A. T K.rnbl-, and it is after all, not very surprising that Warrington were beaten by 147 to 109.

On the Warrington side, Clark, the wicket keeper I tried hard to retrieve the position of affairs, but unfor tunately, he could not find anyone to remain with him, and he carried out his bat for an excellent 28,the highest score of the match on either side. Wordsworth also played well far his 17. Captain Plomer signalised la's appear- ance, in the team by a capital 14, and J. J. Croefield was the fourth do utile figure scorer with 10. A satisfactory item from the Warrington point of view is that although Liverpool scored 147, thPy only obtained 2 extras, where- as, Warringto with 107 had as many as 14.

In the bow Ens,, department, Sharpe of Liverpool came out with wonderful figures, for he obtained two wickets for no runs. R. Smith as is usual, was the most successful bowler for Warrington with four wickets from 41. J. J. Crosfield had three for 37, and E. Connor two for 26, while Bates' single wicket cost as much as the four of Smith. The Liverpool team were very fortumate in the spin of the coin, for the wicket was very" bumpy towards the close of the garne,and (1 course considerably helped the bowlers.

The averages of the Warrington batsmen have suft-red this we, k with one exc..ution, and that is Clark, who with his 28 not out last Siturday very much improved his position on the table. Smith though still at the top, has not such a commanding lead as he had the previous week, and that duck which W.FI. Podmore ' made has also spoiled his average. No one but Smith has yet scored 100 runs, Sates with 84 being secon,l, while his fellow prolessional,Clark, comes third with 61. These are not very good scores considering that seven innings have been played.

The Sankey Wesleyans and Sankey Wire Mills teams each had a draw on Saturday, and had the games been played out, it is not easy to say which would have won, although the Mills team had the best chance. The Wesleyans took on the Penketh Friends, and so stunt:yarn was the game that four and a half hours were not sufficient to decide it. There was some good scoring nn either side, and the bowling averages of all the bow- lers was very much spoiled. Taylor made a capital : stand for the Wesleyans and his 34 WAS of great vAlue to his side, without doubt saving, the game. The Friends are You.gh customers to met, and it is a long time since 100 runs ware scored against them.

The Wire Mills met We.ton,and had the misfortune to find Ker.h.i w in good form, as in bowling, he took five wickets for 15 runs, an I then scored 17. Williams and Cook,the wicket keeper, were the top scsrers for Sankey with 16, and they were closely followed by Marshall 14, and Simpson 12. By he way, there were not s) many Tudors as usual in the Weston te.m, as there were only itwo. Weston seems to be a hotbed of this genus, and I almost a whole team could be made out of them.

The Y.M.C.A. (Ist an I 2ad) continued their victorious career on Saturday,and made the Unity,first and second, look very small. The Unity second are having a parti- cularly had time of it ;tt present,and the avenge of the collectiv. score of their team would not be a very res- pectable 6g ure.

The Panketh Wesleyans had to be content. with a draw nn Stturday, when they placed a team from Widnes. They have not been particularly sticcessful as vet this Reason, but pertvips their turn will come. Thev are meeting the Sankey Wesleyani to-dayorvi a warm game it will be, and whichever wins will deserve their vic- tory.

Lancashire' have carried all before them an far this season, and it will take a strong team to take them down. Their victory over K •nt was very welcome as the four previous matches with Kent had resulted in victories for the hop county. Now that the tables are turned, they have been turned with vengeance, and a 'crushing victory has been inflicted lip in Kent. Paul and Mold were the most useful men for Lancashire, thr. former with the bat and the latter with the ball. Mold, in fact, appears to he in exceptional form this year,and strange to say he can make runs, just when they are most needed, as witness his 57 against Leicestershire, and his 32 this week against Surrey. Briggs is not to the fore as usnal, hut if he were not brought into con- trast with Mold, he would be pretty conspicuous.

Gloucester have not kept up the promise with which thr,37 started, and have had two very bad falls. This is the usual war with one man teams, and when W. G. Grace fails, it is generally "all up" with Gloucester- shire. Instead of heading, the list, they:hive now four counties with better figures.

Surrey are now level with Lancaghire with four points to the good, but th9v have played two matclaes more than Lancashirp. The match between these counties this wo, k, wvl) go a long way toward deciding the cham- pionship this year.

THE Stratford Express has interviewed Mrs. Hayden, of Coborn-road, London, E., who has a well known provision shop there,and has undergone severe sufferings for many months and been expected to die. She said, "IVg 3 3 attacked with spasms round the heart. The pain was dreadful, and although well wrapped up and resting close by the fire, I felt very cold. Sometimes my doctor was here three times a day. My appetite com- pletely left me, and I dreaded the very sight of food. With every attack of the spasms I felt myself to be getting weaker and weaker. It was not safe to leave me alone ; had oto have somebody to watch me. I could not sleep more than an hour of a night, and I sometimes was unable to sit down in a chair. I felt I should not recover and cold not exist much longer. I was suffer.- ing from dyspepsia, spasms of the heart, and extr,me nervous debility. My attention was attrlcted, however y an article in a local newspaper about the great good one to some people by takinff Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale reople, and I commenced to take them. After taking the first box I felt a little better. My appetite seemed to be a little better, and I did not feel so low spirited. I had a strong feeling that I was going to get better. In a few weeks I was able to walk about, and now I can take a good walk, and attend to the business. It is marvellous how I have got so well." The Press Association states that Mr. Broadhurst, rresided on Wednesday evening over a meeting at the House of Commons of the executive committee of the league which is being formed to promote ls.islalion to put an end to the system of tied houses. The pros- pectus of the proposed league was revised, and it was 81 ated that adhesions to the programme continued to come in daily from all parts of the country.
