div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLETOWN.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLETOWN.
SPEECHES BY M. J. MOON, MR. It. W. PERKS, M.P., COUNCILLOR FORSPER, ETC.
A crowded meeting of Liberals was held at the Earles- town Town Hill on Wednesthy evening, to elect repre- . .

sentatives upon the divisional " 30D,"—and also to h. ar addresses from Mr. J. Moon, the Liberal candidate-elect for the Newton diviSion, Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., etc. The routine business was gone through at the commence- ment, and at the meeting subs( vently held, the chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, J.P., and there were al.io present on the platform—Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., Mr. J. Moon, Councillor J. Forster Liberal can- didate for St. Helene, Mr. G. F. Clarke, ;,on. secretary of the Earlestown Liberal Association, the Rev. F. E. Miller and Messrs. W. Gilmour, S. Flarvey, J. H. Profit, and J. Cnrdinglf.y (Etriestown): Messrs. R. Openshaw, and. B. Yates (Gol borne); S. Tither,_. and.. T. Starkey

; Dr. Latham and Mr. J. Mitchell (Ashton)-; the Rev. J. H. Riddette. Dr. D,)wling, Messrs. J.Latham, .1. R ,berts and J. G. Mullins (Ilaydo_k). Mr. Rawlins in his opening speech said that he wa4 sorry that Mr. E iward Evans, jun.' was not with them that evening. Be had sent the following letter : "I am sorry I cannot be at tee meeting held at Earlestown on Wednesday next. I regret that I have to go to Lnndon . . . . . .

to attend in important-meeting of the Nat;Mal Liberal Federation Committee on that day. I am glad to see that Mr. Perks is to address you—(applause)—as he him- self has shown what can be done in constituencies by hard work. I can assure you that keen interest is being takm at head quarters in what is being done in the Newton Division, and I know that intense satisfaction would be felt, if you confirm the candidature of my ' friend, Mr. Moon, who is as I know a thorough going radical, and will be able to give expression of the reason cf the faith that is in him. Trusting you will have a slicce,‘Fiful meeting, an with best wishes, I am, etc.. EDWARD Eveass Jun." (Applaose ) Continuing. the .Chairman said diat while they regretted that Mr. Evans was not with them that night, they saw that he Was doing useful work elsewhere. He thought that they might look upon that day in Earlestown, as a red letter day for Liberalism. They had upon the platform that night, on- present and two future members of Pirlia- ment., (Applause.) That was Mr. Perks' first appear- ance upon a platform in the Newton division, and they cordially welcomed him. (Apolause.) By reput- ation, he was knArn by all there, as one of those hard working sincere and able Liberals who helped to carry on the great work of the country. With regard to Mr. Moon all he would say was that they would know him better soon. (Applause.) It had ben his agreeable duty to go a good deal abut the consti- tuency with Mr. Moon, and he could tell them what he thought about him, but he would spare his blushes on that occasion. (Laughter.) He, however, felt certain of this—what when they knew Mr. Moon as well as he knew him, they would only be too glad to choose him a candidate at the next contest in the Newton division. (Applause.) Mr. Moon's Liberalism was like Cm3ar's wife—above suspicion. and it was strong ar9 robust, . . -

and just the kind of Liberalism which would bring a man at the head of the poll. With regard to Mr. Fors- ter, he was the future Liberal member for a neighbour- ing constitneniy—(applause),—and they were heartily glad to see him there that night. Mr. Forster was too well known there for it to be necessary fer him to sty anything about him. It Was good to sees large Liberal meeting like that at such times as the present. There was a spirit of unrest abroad, a kind of a scare with re- gard to a general election. That very great authority, the " Times" (laughter) told them that there was likely to be a general election in July. Well, generally speak- ing, he would say that the " Times " always falsified its own prophecy and a very good evidence that there will be no election in July was that the " Times "said there would be. (Laughter.) But they knew that if a man was told systematically by his friends that he was look- ing ill, in a short time, he would believe he was ill. (Laughter) And at present the Liberals were being told by the "Times " and the Tories, and all other adverse organisations that there was going to be a general election in July, and many timid Liberals conerquently believed there would be one. He would say that the present Government was one of the best governments of modern times. It knew what it was about, it knew what it wanted and what the constituencies wanted, and had kept a plain straighforwarel course before it, and he saw no reason why it should dissolve because the Tories wanted a die- solution. Their position was about as bad as it could be, and they were there'nre anxious to take the off chance of a victory at the next general election. The unfortunate Liberal dissentient wanted one too (Laugh- ter) as. they were very small in numbers, and could not be very much smaller. There was another august body which wanted a dissolutions, and that was the Rouse of Lords. He hoped it would be lout; before the country responded to the wishes of the House of Lords. In connection with this he was reminded of a song in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera, " lolanthe," in which it said " When Wellington beat Bunnaparte, as everyone can tell; the House of Lords throughout the war, did nothing in particular and did it very well." (Laughter.) As long Is the House of Lords did nothing in particular they did it very well, but the moment it began to do something in particular, it made a great mess of it. (Applause.) It was however their duty to be prepared tor a dissotullnn at any time, and they wanted to have their candidate out, and to have their organisation com- plete. and their registration attended to, and then, when the diseolution came, they would be ready. (Ap- planse.) Mr. J Latham moved the following resolution: "That this meeting expresses its entire confidence in the pre- sent government, and hereby congratulates them upon the excellent measures they have passed, and trusts they will endeavour to pass the measures of reform contained in the Newcastle programme." He said that the present member for Newton told them the government were simply plontehing the sands, hut if they could produce by this praetice such crone as they had done, he hoped thee would continue to ploueh the sands. (Applause.) Mr. .T. Moon,who was received with loud applause, in seconding the resolution, thanked the meeting for the encouragement they had given him on making his first appearance at E irlesrown. The privilege of seconding Inc resolution, he had no hesitation in undertakints, he. cause he knew that in any meeting of good Liberals it would not only be well received, but would meet with a hearty and entliesiastic reception. In the short time he had been cr.nnected with the Newton division, he had already found that notwithstanding the long dreary reign of Toryism in the district, there existed at the same time a very strong and powerful Liberal element —(hear, hear, and applause)—an element which he seri- ously believed was so strong and so powerful that, it weasel very soon assert itself, and put an end to the long Tory aecendencv by returning some fine day a Liberal to the Honse of Commons. (Loud applause.) He hoped that the day was not far distant, and he also hoped that he might be there to see and to share in it. (Loud ap- plause.) Since his friend, Mr. Rawlins first approached him with a view to meeting the executive of the Liberal 1 Arreneiation.he had noticed two things about the Newton division. It was said that lookers on saw meet of the LI (same. He noticed first, that there were many local Liberals in Newten, who by no means tinder-estimated the strength of Toryism, and they seemed to think that Lit was a drea Thal thing to challenge it. All he had to l say to !het Was that it Was all the more reason why they should fight it—(hear, hear) —because, after all, the cause of Liberalism always had been an uphill fiehteend always would he. Their fathers found it an uphill fight to carry the great Reform Act of 1832, and also the ad- mission of Catholics into the Rouse of Commons, or dis- senters to the Universities. But he did not think they were daunted because it was an uphill fight. When the time came in Newton division for their courage to be put to the test, he did not think they would he daunted. (Applause.) On the contrary, he believed 1 that it would make every Liberal in the division to work all the harder in support of hie principles. They met that night in support of the present Government who needed all the encouragement they could give them. ' The presence of Mr. Perks that night was an evidence of the interest their leaders were taking in them. as the Chairman had informed them, Mr. Perks was known as a philanthropic worker in every cause for the ameliora- tion and improvement of the workers of the country,and his generosity in many a needy ease was well known to 'many of them. He supposed his Conservative friends would say he was blind when he said that he really did not think it was a difficult matter to defend the present Government. The measures introduced during the short time of its existence had been very democratic, and but for the House of Leris,many useful Bills would have been passed. (Hear, hear.) But the measures they had already reseed, slush as the graduation of the death duties the equalisation of those duties, and the Parish Councils Bill would alone justify their claim to the sup- port of the country. (Applause.) Lord Salisbury had said that the Government had only a majority of five, and vet there were measures like the Welsh Disestablish- ment Bill which were passed by a majority of over 40,50 that the Tories must be very lukewarm and indifferent to the Bill which thee described as " spAiation and rob- lsery of God." (Oh ! Oh ! ) They would, however, rally round to try to defeat the Local Veto Bill when it came to be discussed. That Bill, they described as being the robbery of the publican. They appeared to regard the rehbery of tke publiean as much more serious than the former. (Hear, hear.) The publican was of course an important element in the matter. Brewers not only bicker] their interest With votes bet also with herd cash, and a very great number of Conservative members supported the church, the constitution and the empire, but last and greatest of all, the public-houses, (Applause 1 They were told they would be defeated on the Local Veto Bill. Well, he could say that he did not think they could have a better question to go to the country upon than the Local Veto Bill—(applause),_ because he believed that there were thousands of men, =mien of those who drank not wisely hut ton well—he thought thee even those would vote for the reduction of facilities fer drinking. (Rear. hear.) Th.. Bill was simply giving the people the power maeisrretee had at the pres- sit tinte, and the cause of Conservative opposition was
itself to use its best endeavours to promote the return of a Liberal candidate for the Newton division." Mr. Mullins seconded the resolution.

Councillor F.nster ta..artily supported the resolution. He said that the present Govern;nmt deserved the sup- port of none more than an industrial constituency like Newton. He had had much amusement at the remarks of the member for the division, and to judge from wrist he hael seer. ir the papers, they themselves were net very mach s'7.ruck with the intellectual power of their member of Parliament. (Laughter.) He thou.dot that , the man to represent a constituency was the one who ' was most in sympathy with the people who were in it —(applause)—and he hoped that the Newton divi:ion would return Nfr.Moon as its representative. Mr. Fors- ter then proceeded to speak of the general policy of the party, and urged that great stress should he laid up )n the Rood administrative work of governme it. The res,ylutien was then pat to the meeting and car- ried unanimously. The meeting was afterwards brought to a close with the usual votes of thanks.
NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Earlestown Town Flail on Monday. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided, and there were also present, Messrs. E. T. Evans, W. Beatty J. Sle9 J. W. Emmett J. Smeth, J.
Simpson, T. Ortna'nd, W. l-iilmour, F. Wood, W. Thornp- son, jun., R Stone, P. INtlAcMahon, W. Collingwood, Rev. E. W. W. Klye, Messrs. J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Morley (.!li.rk and surveyor.
TEE APF)INTERNT OF OVER,RERS -MR. GILMORE AND THE LAW CLERK. _

After the adoption cf the minutes of the previous meeting had been proposed and 6econded, Mr. Gihnour said that before they wore put to the meeting, he would like to ask a question with reference to the appointment of overseers. They would remember no doubt that dis- cussions had taken place from time to time with refer- ence to that appointment. No doubt the law clerk hid the memorandum of the Local Government Board as to the numb •r which condi be appointed. Their law clerk had told them that no more than two could be ap- pointed. He (Mr. Gihnour) however, had it from the Local Government B ,ard that there could not be less than two, nor more than four. He knew of one place where three hat been eecte-1, and also another where four were elected. He would like to know what was the law clerk's opinion. He thought he had a perfect right to make this explanation, He had contradicted the law clerk, and .he mie,lit be considered a nuisance in acting thus. He therefore wished is to go to the public that the Local Government Board memorandum stated that not less than two nor more than four overseers could be appointed. . - .
The Cniirman : Rave you written to the Local, Government fi,)ard and received a reply from them 2
Mr. Giltnur: I haw, their memorandum.
The Chair nan : That is another matter. Mr. Smith : Tula question has been settled. We are only taking up the time of the Counnil. Mr. Gilmour : I will allsw any member to see the memorandum.
The Law Clerk; We all have a memorandum. Mr. Gll[llol2l' Will you say whether we can appoint more than two oververs

Mr.- Ma.:Ma. hon : I put that question at the last meetinz. I p t it distinctly in the face of this Board, and the an swer was that we could not,. I said that I believed we could, but before I had finished I was ruled out of order.
Mr. Smith : lam quite sure that if we wish, we can elect two, three, or f,,ur. Mr. GI !moor: That was contradicted at our last meetinv. . . .

The dnairmtn was about to put the minutes to the meetins,i,when Mr.Einmett interrupting said that hetore they were passed he thlught the LAW Clerk should either put himself right, or say that he still held thio same opinion. 119 thought that Mr. Gilmour had a perfect right to raiqi this question. Mr. Gilmour : I move that we have an answer from the Law Clerk before the minutes are passed. Mr. Gil mour Was proceeding with somo further observations- when Mr. Smith called " Order," whPreupr n Mr. Gil, moor indignantly cried out" Is Mr. Smith the chairmAn or you sir. I think M. Smith ought to have more man ners than ti 4 act as he does."
The Chairman : I a4k you to At down. Mr. G.lmour : I will sir for you, but not for this gen- tletnin hem _

The Chairman then put the minutes to the Connell, and Mr. Smith claimed th it the " Ayes had it." Mr. Gilmour, however,challenoed it, and a division was then taken. The following voted that the minutes were ac- curate : Mews. Collingwood, Wood, Stelne, Simoson, Smith, Thomnson, Sipe and IC +ye, ; against, Meqsrs. Emmett, M!cNithon, Gilmour, Beatty, Evans, and Orm ttid, 6 --The minutes were, therefore, adopted.

div.head: THE" EXAMINER "CALLED OVER THE COALE.
div.p: THE" EXAMINER "CALLED OVER THE COALE.

Before the minutes of the various committees were considered, Mr. Emmett said that he wished to bring before the notice of the Council, that in the EarleAtown " Examiner," the minutes were already published. He wanted to know by whose authority those minute were published. Re thought it was a 'very wrong thing that , they should be published before they were confirmed by . that Council. The Chairman said that he was not in a position to say by whose authority the minutes were published. fie ' had a distinct recollection of a nunsher of gentlemen voting that the p-ess Should he admitted to the meetings of the committee, and he thought that the gentleman who had just asked that cpestion was one of them him- , soli, he (the chairman) saw no objection to the minutes I b-ing published. They had to he confirmed afterwards. i There could not be any objection to it. As to the authoitv 1 or how the" Examiner" gained the information, he did not say how it was gained. Mr. MarMlhon said that he was in favour of the press being admitted to the committee meeting,s.hut he did not belies' ein favour. There should be no favour at all. fla did not think it right that any member should carry in- formation to his favourite paper. Mr. Gilmuur spoke in a similar strain. The Chairman suggested that the Law Clerk should explain the matter. The Law Clerk then explained that by a resolution of the Council, it was decided that the minutes of the elm;
. , . mittees shaold he printed 3nd sent to each rnemhcr of the C uncil and also to each newsonanr in the district. The minutasi were accordingly sent to the reporter of
eanh paper in the ditrict. Mr. Gilmour again rose to speak. but the Chairman ruled him out oF ord .1., and declared the matter closed.
HIGHWAYS COMMITTRH.-SETTS V. MACADAM!

The minutes of this committee whl3ll were published in our las issue, were moved by Mr. Collingwood, seconded by Mr. Stone. Mr. Ormand called attention to the following resolution passed by the committee : " The report of the sub-com- mittee te consider the making of private streets, dated 13-h May, wag read, and after a prolonged discussion on setts and macadam, it was adopted." tie said that he thought that more information shoubld he given than i there was in that paragraph. The Council should be told what the sub.committee intended to do. I A lootr discussion of shout an hour's duration now ensued and it was elicited that it was intended to pave a large number of streets with macadam. ' Mr. Wood spoke strongly in favour of setts,contending that even the original cost for macadam would be very little less than the cost of laying setts, while the cost of maintenance would he eight times greater. In addition to this a steam roller would be required which would cost something llae £3OO. An amendment WAS finally moved hy Mr. Ormand and seconded by Mr. Emmett, that the report upon street making no referred bank to the sub-committee for further consideration and that they further report thereon. This Was pill; to the vote, and the following members supported it: Messrs. Emmett, Gllmore, Wood, Slee and Ormand, 5 ; against, Messrs. Collingwood, ManMahon, Stone, Simnkon, Smith, Thompson, Kaye, Beatty and Evans, 9. The amendment was therefore lost. Mr. Collin 'wood then moved and Mr. Beatty seconded that a certain number of streets which were named, be paved with macadam at the cost of the property- owners. Mr. W rod nr..ved and Mr. Emmett seconded that they be paved with setts. The following vo'el for setts : Messrs. Emmett, Gil, mom% Wool, slee, and Ormond-5; for macadam, Messrs. Collingwood, MacMahon, Stone, Simpson,Smith roomoson. Kaye. Beatty, and Evans-9. The streets will therefore be paved with macadam. NEWTON TOLLS. With reference to the tolls collected at Newton Com- mon on the occasion flf the May Day festival, the Law Clerk said that he hal seen Mr. Parties", who said that he collected stallage rents, from nernale who occupied the land which belonged to Lord Nowton.by right. He held that the Council had no right to collect tolls. Mr. Ormanl sail that he thought the Council ought to dispute that as it was a question of common tolls. Mr. MacMahon moved and Mr. Ormand seconded that the matter be referred to the committee for further con- sideration and this was passed unanimously. THR ACCIDENT AT RYAN'S CROSSING.

-..-- - A letter was read from Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, calling the attention 'of the Council to a pre- sentment made by the jury which sat at an inquest recently held. This °resentment was to the effect that a nvenary should be provided by the District Council. Mr. Scone sugv,ested that a letter be sent to Mr. Shaw asking him to send a ,t:ortfr to the crossing of Messrs Richard Evans and Company when any wavgons were Wren aeross it to prevent any further accidents, as the crosaing was very dangerous. Mr. Gilmour thought this a proper reconsmendation. tie also thought that the j ury's presentment should he attended to. On the motion of Mr. Orman& seconded by Mr. Col- iingwood, the letter from Mr. Brighouse was referred to the flivh ways Committee. Mr. Evans thought that Mr. Stone's suggestion with regard to Evans' crossings was a very good one, and moved that a !otter be sent to Mr. Shaw requesting him to carry the suggestion into effect. Mr. MacMalson seconded the resolution, which was passed unanimously. AN ALLEGED TRESPASS BY THE COUNCIL.
A letter was read frond Mr. Pardey, Lord Newton%

div.head: CLAIM FOR, THE MAINTENANCE OF A CHILD.
div.p: CLAIM FOR, THE MAINTENANCE OF A CHILD.
PECULIAR CASE:

Thomas Smith Paul was sued at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffouikes, by his wife Emma Paul, residing in Marson-at., Warringtm, hr £9 153., for the mainten- ance of her son, during 39 weeks, at ss. per weok. Mr. Arthur Browne, who appeared on behalf of the plaintiff, said that tne Parties for some time lived in Warrington, but subsequently removed to Crosby, hear Liverpool. In consequence of her husnand's ill-usage, the plaintiff was compelled to leave defendant and come home to her mother who was residing in Maeson-st. She had lived in Warrington since October 1893, and laid kept herself. She had one child who was for time kept by the defendant. Oa May 4th 1894, plaintiff received a letter from her hus- band, then in Crosby, asking her if she would keep the child as he (defendant) was out of work, and it was breaking his heart to know that their son was not hav- ing enough to eat. The letter continued that if the plaintiff had still a spark of motherly feeling for her son, she would consent to keep the lad until defendant again got into work. As soon as hs procured work he pro- mised to write to her and pay for the maintenance of the boy. Plaintiff replied on May 5, saying she would have the boy if defendant would pay her. In reply to this letter she received one from her husband again saying that he would pay for the lad's maintenance. Tne child was sent by train about five weeks later, and plaintiff had maintained him ever since. The defendant had had two amounts on account, one being ss. and the other £l. Suiddenly,the defendant disappeared,and the plaintiff did not hear anything of it until some time ago she was informed that he was in a good nosi- ness at Rhyl. He had been approached but refused to pay for the maintenance, saying that he wanted the child handed over to him. The child was, however, suffering from a very severe complaint, and was consequently not in a fit condition to he placed in the custody of the father.—The Judge said that the father could claim the child but at his own risk—Emma! Paul supported her solicitor's statement. She said that she had spent a great deal of money in procuring cloth- ing, education, and food for the lad, and during his ill- ness he had medical attendance, an account for which had not been rendered. He was still being attended by a doctor.—Mr. Watkins Wynne Parry, solicitor, Rhyl, for the defendant said that it was impossible for his client t, appear. He was anxious and willing to keep the child, and being a sober,respectable and kindly man, he was quite entitled to the custody of the child, and he was,according to law, the proper custodian of the child. —His Honour That has no belting upon the case which is a claim for maintensnce.—Mr. Parry : He is able to keep the boy if he is given up, as a matter of fact, he has made terms to keep the boy, but the mother has re- fused.—The Judge said that the action was practically undefended. The defendant had authorised the plain- tiff to maintain the la.f on condition that he (defendant) would pay her. The sum of Bs. per week as charged by the plaintiff was not too much for the nquirements of :11 hey, and he would, therefore, give judgment for £9 154., the full amount c'aimed.

div.head: BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDHNT.
div.p: BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDHNT.

The net deed of what in future will be known as Malcom Guild Hall was uoanimly approved of at a conference at which Sir .1. T. Brunner met the representatives of the various societies which it is intended to benefit. The fli ft of the hall, the cost of which has exceeded £2,000, is another in- stance of ir J. T. Brunner's interest in the welfare of the people. The premises are to he used for , meetinZS of trades' unions, labourers' unions, friendly and provident and other kindred societies, and for the promotion of relisious, educational, ' temperance, political,and recreative purposes. This surely is a most inclusivs=phrase, and it c innot. in future, he said that such organisations are crippled for want of asnitable meeting place. The situation and arrangements of the hall make it an ideal place for the purposes for which it, is intended. In the past a diffi,mlty has been experienced by some of the societies mentioned in consequence of having to meet in public-houses, where the presence of drink has been a drawback in the transaction of the business. But no such diffimity will exist at the Guild Hall, for a clause in the trust, deed pro- vides that no alcoholic Ihquors or intoxicating drinks are to he consurn-d on the premises. It now remains for the members of the societies to make the hall what the donor intended it to be—a home of unity, concord, and mutual helpfulness.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, nine youths ' were summoned for gambling at a refreshment , house, or to be more exact, at a fried fish and chipped potato shop. It appears that they were card playing at a game called " Brag" for half- pence, and were caught doing so by three police officers. The law was of course set in motion and the youths were brought before the magistrates and punished—or at least their parents were—by paying the costs which were imposed. But does it not seem rather a reflection on the presumed equal justice existing in England when these lads for their halfpenny gambling are placed in the police box, and yet habitual betting men, book- makers, and turf swindlers generally, are seldom, if ever, placed in a similar position? These lads farm but a part of the outer fringe of that large circle of gamblers who are to be found in every town in the country, but still they usually become the scape- goats for the rest.

There was a long discussion at the meeting of the Runcorn School Board on Tuesday as to whether the number of members should be in- creased from seven to nine, and on a vote being taken the chairman's resolution proposing to apply for sanction to increase the number was defeated by one vote. It cannot be said that the arguments brought against the proposition were particularly strong ; it was the old Conservative doctrine that things are right as they are, and that any change is unnecessary. On the other hand it was pointed out that wih the transfer of the Wesleyan schools to the Board, increased work would follow, and, further, that Runcorn when compared with other towns had fewer members upon the School Board than the majority of places. Then again from what fell from the lips of some of the members it was not criite clear that the work was being carried out as serenely as might be wished, as there seems to be some little difficulty occasionally in forming a School Attendance Committee. Altogether there seemed to be strong grounds for increasing the number of members but as a majority of the Board has thought otherwise, the ratepayers of Runcorn will be continued to be represented by seven.

It will he remembered that at last week's council meeting, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi mentioned that the Ship Canal Company were charging a toll for cross- ing the Canal by the ferry. The Law Clerk advised people not to pay it, and the rev, gentleman has this week been testing the matter. He proceeded by the ferry across the Canal, but when he reached the opposite side be was asked for the fare. This he refused to pay, with tte result that when Dr. Gastaldi again presented himself as a passenger for the ferry at a later date, the ferryman declined to take him across the waterway. It will thus be seen that the Canal Company seem determined to con- tinue the toll, and the sooner the points at issue are settled, the better. It is satisfactory to learn that a conference is to be held on Wednesday at which representatives of the London and North-Western Railway Company, the Ship Canal Company, and the Runcorn and Widnes Councils will be present. If no definite arrangement is come to concerning the ferry, the application for restitution of the alleged public rights will be made at the forthcom- ing Assizes.

A BOOKFOR MARRIED WOMEN. The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, and it will not harm the unmarried to read. The book is c ,aveoiently divided into 12 a hapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. Tho second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age for mart 'age, and who should hive children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only from an listen gent duct.. The third eh .pter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four tre lts of the signs of pregnancy. The filth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. The sixth chapter treats of mishaps and how to avoid them The seventh chapter treats of maternal impressions and shows that birthm arks are not due to longings n the part of the mother, 11.. it rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy i certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chaeter treats of sterility ; tives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the " change," a.. most important article for at women over forty. The book is full of useful information, and no book is w Men which goes so thoroughly into matters relating to ruarrie l women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the ca,e, for knowledge is power , and the means a attaining happiness. The book can be had from Dr. T. R. ALLINSON, 25 Box, 4, Spanish-place, Manchester-square, London, W., in return for a Postal Order for Is. Id.

MEEID G OF WA lt RINUTON INS LT lt ANCE AGENTS. A meeting of the insurance agents of Warrington was held at the Buckley-st. schoolroom on Wednesday we, k, for the purpose of protesting against the Insurance of Children Bill which has been introduced by Sir Richard Webster into the House of Commons, at the in- stance of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and which has already passed the second reading. The part of the Bill which is most strongly objected to by the insurance agents is dance 7 which while allowing affiliated societies to insure chil- dren twelve months old, will prohibit collecting, socie- ties such as the Prudential, Royal Liver, Pearl, etc.,frora doing so under two yearsef age. The Bill also proposes to lower the amount whereby a child may be insured. The chair at the meeting was occupied by Mr. W. Ash- croft, who, in a somewhat lengthy speech. pointed out the unfairness and injustice which he said would be caused by this Bill if it were pass d into law. lie said that it would be a great blow to the business of the friendly societies, and also a great injustice to the poor people of the country who could not afford to bury their children unless they received aid from the insurance societies. Mr. P. Delaney moved a resolution calling upon Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., Sir William Harcourt, and Mr. Balfour to do their utmost to prevent the Bill irons becoming law. He said that the returns of GI? Registrar General tor the past 40 years showed that the state of affairs in matters relating to insurance of children had not altered, and though so many small children had been insured, the cases of child murder were exceedingly small—in fact, so small that they did net call for .tny legislative action. Hl' contended that the Bill was a reflc4on upon the working people of the cow., ry, and that it -s-as a questions which they should take up. He hoped that the meetings which were held in various parts of the country would have the effect of kitting; the Bill which was as uncalled for as it was un- just. Mr. B. Hobson, of Pt.nketh, seconded the resolu- tion, which was passed unanimously. Messrs. Hobson, Ashcroft, and Delaney were appointed a committee to deal with all matters relating to this Bill. Attention was also called at the meeting to an illegal practice which it was alleged was carried out by women chiefly in public-houses, in which imeirance money was handed over to parents of a deceased child without the in des- sary registrar's certificate being produced as req mired by law. It was contended that t is mattrr ought to be brought before the proper authorities and put a stop to. The meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.
